Pattern 12 of 24

Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Explore in rings: first everything 1 step away, then everything 2 steps away, and so on. Because of that, the first time BFS reaches a node is guaranteed to be by a shortest route.

1. What is this pattern for?

Drop a pebble in a still pond. The ripple reaches every point 1 cm away, then every point 2 cm away, and so on. It never skips ahead. Whatever the ripple touches first, it touched by the shortest route. Drop several pebbles at once and you get multi-source BFS: each point is reached by its nearest pebble.

BFS works on any graph (nodes joined by edges): a road map, a social network, a grid of cells, or an implicit graph where the "nodes" are states (lock combinations, words) and an "edge" is one legal move. It uses a queue: first in, first out, like a line at a coffee shop. Nodes are served in the order they were discovered, which means in order of distance.

Use it for:

  • Shortest path / fewest moves when every move costs the same (unweighted).
  • Level-by-level processing: "after k minutes", "k degrees of separation".
  • Multi-source spreading: fire, infection, rotting, "distance to the nearest X".
  • Topological order by peeling (Kahn's algorithm / peeling leaves).

2. How it works (bisected)

  1. Seed the queue. Put the start node in a deque, set dist[start] = 0, and mark it seen.
  2. Pop from the front. u = queue.popleft(). Because of FIFO order, u is always one of the closest nodes not yet expanded.
  3. Discover neighbours. For each neighbour v not yet seen: set dist[v] = dist[u] + 1, remember parent[v] = u, mark it seen right now, and push it to the back.
  4. Repeat until the queue is empty (or until you pop the target). The queue always holds at most two neighbouring distances, d and d+1. That's why the rings never get out of order.
  5. Need levels? Freeze size = len(queue) and pop exactly size nodes per round. Each round is one level (one minute, one move).
  6. Many starting points? Put all of them in the queue at distance 0 before the loop. That's multi-source BFS, and it costs the same as a single BFS.
  7. Need the path itself? Walk parent pointers back from the target, then reverse.

3. Seeing a problem: how to spot BFS

Trigger words

  • "shortest path", "minimum number of steps / moves / turns / transformations"
  • "fewest", "nearest", "closest", "distance to the nearest…"
  • "after each minute", "spreads to adjacent", "level by level", "degrees of separation"
  • "all of them at the same time" (several sources) → multi-source BFS
  • "one letter / one digit / one move at a time" → implicit state graph

Shape of the input

  • A graph or grid where every move costs 1 (no weights, or all weights equal).
  • A start state and a goal state, plus a rule that generates neighbour states.
  • Brute-force smell: trying DFS over all paths and keeping the minimum (exponential), or running a separate BFS from every source (O(k·(V+E))) when one multi-source BFS would do.
The one question to ask"Is this asking for the minimum number of equal-cost steps?" If yes, BFS. If the steps have different costs, use Dijkstra (a BFS with a heap, see Top K / heaps).

4. When to use it, and when not to

Use BFS when…Prefer something else when…
Shortest path / fewest moves, every edge costs the sameEdges have different weights: use Dijkstra (heap, see Top K Elements). 0/1 weights: 0-1 BFS with a deque
Answers grouped by distance or time (levels)You just need reachability / components / cycles: DFS is shorter to write and works just as well
Several sources spreading at onceYou need all paths or all combinations: Backtracking
Per-level questions on a binary treeOrder-dependent tree work (inorder, postorder sums): Tree Traversal
Grids of cells with 4/8-direction movesSee Matrix Traversal for boundary and direction-vector tricks
Very wide but shallow search spacesThe graph is very deep and memory is tight: DFS uses O(depth) memory while BFS uses O(width)

Cost: O(V + E) time and O(V) space (queue + seen). On an R × C grid that's O(R·C). In implicit state graphs, V = number of reachable states (e.g. 104 lock codes).

5. The templates, step by step (Python, TypeScript, Java)

BFS has four templates, all built on one queue that is processed oldest-first. Because nodes leave the queue in order of distance, the first time BFS reaches a node is along a shortest path (in an unweighted graph). A records each node's distance. B groups nodes into levels. C remembers each node's parent to rebuild the actual shortest path. D starts from several sources at once ("rotting oranges", nearest exit). The graph is an adjacency list: graph[node] lists the neighbours.

Template A · Distances from one source

The question it answersHow many edges is each node from src (unweighted)?
What it keepsdist: node → distance; doubles as the visited set. A FIFO queue.
When it checks for an answerA node's distance is set the moment it's discovered, never changed.
Use it whenShortest path length in unweighted graphs/grids, word ladder, minimum moves/steps.
Not forWeighted edges (Dijkstra, page 20); 0/1 weights (0-1 BFS with a deque).
Memory hook: "Ripples in a pond: everything at distance 1, then 2, then 3"Drop a stone at the source. The ripple reaches all neighbours first, then their neighbours. The first ripple that touches a node is the shortest way there, so you write its distance down once and never again.

The story, mapped to the code. The source is where the stone lands.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
Where the stone landsdist[src] = 0Distance 0.
Ripple front waiting to spreadqueueOldest first (FIFO).
Ripple touches a dry spotneighbour not in distDiscovered for the first time.
Write its ring numberdist[neighbour] = dist[current] + 1One more than the node it came from.
It will spread laterqueue.append(neighbour)Joins the back of the line.

The template. Set the distance when you enqueue, not when you dequeue.

from collections import deque

def bfs_distances(graph, src):
    dist = {src: 0}
    queue = deque([src])
    while queue:
        current = queue.popleft()
        for neighbour in graph[current]:
            if neighbour not in dist:
                dist[neighbour] = dist[current] + 1
                queue.append(neighbour)
    return dist
function bfsDistances(graph: number[][], src: number): Map<number, number> {
  const dist = new Map<number, number>([[src, 0]]);
  const queue = [src];
  for (let head = 0; head < queue.length; head++) {
    const current = queue[head];
    for (const neighbour of graph[current]) {
      if (!dist.has(neighbour)) {
        dist.set(neighbour, dist.get(current)! + 1);
        queue.push(neighbour);
      }
    }
  }
  return dist;
}
static Map<Integer, Integer> bfsDistances(List<List<Integer>> graph, int src) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> dist = new HashMap<>();
    dist.put(src, 0);
    Deque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(src));
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int current = queue.poll();
        for (int neighbour : graph.get(current)) {
            if (!dist.containsKey(neighbour)) {
                dist.put(neighbour, dist.get(current) + 1);
                queue.offer(neighbour);
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

Line by line.

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves
dist = {src: 0}The source is discovered at distance 0.The stone lands.Forgetting it lets the source be "discovered" again from a neighbour at distance 2.
current = queue.popleft()Oldest first.Spread the oldest ripple.pop() is a stack: DFS order, distances become wrong (see Template C's bug player).
if neighbour not in distOnly undiscovered nodes.Dry spot?—
dist[neighbour] = dist[current] + 1; queue.append(neighbour)Mark on discovery.Write the ring number now.Marking on dequeue lets the same node be enqueued many times (slow, and wrong if you set the distance at push time without the check).

Watch it run. Step through BFS from node 0. Node 3 is reachable from both 1 and 2; watch it get its distance once.

Dry run (generated from the same trace as the first player above):

Invariant. The queue holds nodes in non-decreasing distance order (at most two distinct values, d and d + 1), and every node in dist has its true shortest distance.

Complexity. O(n + m) time, O(n) space.

Mistakes this template invites:

  • Marking visited on dequeue. Write the ring number when the ripple first touches.
  • Using a list's pop(0) in Python. deque.popleft() is O(1).
  • BFS on weighted edges. Ripples assume every edge has length 1.

Template B · Level by level

The question it answersGroup nodes by distance (levels), or answer per-level questions.
What it keepsseen; a queue holding exactly one level at the start of each round.
When it checks for an answerEach round snapshots len(queue) and processes exactly that many.
Use it whenWord ladder length, minimum generations, "nodes at distance k", rotting oranges minutes (with D).
Not forWhen only distances are needed (A is simpler).
Memory hook: "One ring at a time: count the ring before spreading it"Same ripples, but you stop between rings. Count how many points are on the current ring, spread exactly those, and everything they touch forms the next ring.

The story, mapped to the code. Each round is one ring of the ripple.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
Points on this ringlevel_size = len(queue)Snapshot.
Spread one pointcurrent = queue.popleft()Exactly level_size times.
Next ringqueue.append(neighbour)Waits for the next round.
Ring finishedlevels.append(level)One list per ring.

The template. Template A plus the level-size snapshot (the same trick as tree level order, page 10).

from collections import deque

def bfs_levels(graph, src):
    levels, seen = [], {src}
    queue = deque([src])
    while queue:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(queue)):
            current = queue.popleft()
            level.append(current)
            for neighbour in graph[current]:
                if neighbour not in seen:
                    seen.add(neighbour)
                    queue.append(neighbour)
        levels.append(level)
    return levels
function bfsLevels(graph: number[][], src: number): number[][] {
  const levels: number[][] = [], seen = new Set([src]);
  let queue = [src];
  while (queue.length > 0) {
    const next: number[] = [];
    for (const current of queue) {
      for (const neighbour of graph[current]) {
        if (!seen.has(neighbour)) {
          seen.add(neighbour);
          next.push(neighbour);
        }
      }
    }
    levels.push(queue);
    queue = next;
  }
  return levels;
}
static List<List<Integer>> bfsLevels(List<List<Integer>> graph, int src) {
    List<List<Integer>> levels = new ArrayList<>();
    Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>(List.of(src));
    Deque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(src));
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int k = queue.size(); k > 0; k--) {
            int current = queue.poll();
            level.add(current);
            for (int neighbour : graph.get(current)) {
                if (seen.add(neighbour)) {
                    queue.offer(neighbour);
                }
            }
        }
        levels.add(level);
    }
    return levels;
}

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves

levels.append(level)Closes the ring.Ring done.—

Template C · The shortest path itself (parent pointers)

The question it answersReturn the actual shortest path from src to dst.
What it keepsparent: node → the node it was discovered from (doubles as visited).
When it checks for an answerStop when dst is dequeued; walk parents back to src and reverse.
Use it whenPath reconstruction (word ladder II simplified, maze route), any "return the route" prompt.
Not forWeighted graphs (Dijkstra + parents).
Memory hook: "Each node remembers who told it the news"News spreads from the source. Every person remembers who told them. To find the fastest chain to a person, follow "who told you?" back to the source, then read the chain forwards.

The story, mapped to the code. The ripple carries a note: who sent it.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
Who told you?parent[neighbour] = currentRecorded on discovery.
The source heard it firstparent[src] = NoneEnd of the chain.
Follow the chain backwhile step is not None: step = parent[step]dst → … → src.
Read it forwardspath[::-1]src → dst.

The template. Template A with parent instead of dist.

from collections import deque

def shortest_path(graph, src, dst):
    parent = {src: None}
    queue = deque([src])
    while queue:
        current = queue.popleft()
        if current == dst:
            path = []
            while current is not None:
                path.append(current)
                current = parent[current]
            return path[::-1]
        for neighbour in graph[current]:
            if neighbour not in parent:
                parent[neighbour] = current
                queue.append(neighbour)
    return None
function shortestPath(graph: number[][], src: number, dst: number): number[] | null {
  const parent = new Map<number, number | null>([[src, null]]);
  const queue = [src];
  for (let head = 0; head < queue.length; head++) {
    let current: number | null = queue[head];
    if (current === dst) {
      const path: number[] = [];
      while (current !== null) {
        path.push(current);
        current = parent.get(current)!;
      }
      return path.reverse();
    }
    for (const neighbour of graph[current]) {
      if (!parent.has(neighbour)) {
        parent.set(neighbour, current);
        queue.push(neighbour);
      }
    }
  }
  return null;
}
static List<Integer> shortestPath(List<List<Integer>> graph, int src, int dst) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> parent = new HashMap<>();
    parent.put(src, null);
    Deque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(src));
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        Integer current = queue.poll();
        if (current == dst) {
            List<Integer> path = new ArrayList<>();
            while (current != null) {
                path.add(current);
                current = parent.get(current);
            }
            Collections.reverse(path);
            return path;
        }
        for (int neighbour : graph.get(current)) {
            if (!parent.containsKey(neighbour)) {
                parent.put(neighbour, current);
                queue.offer(neighbour);
            }
        }
    }
    return null;
}

Line by line.

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves
parent = {src: None}The source has no parent; also marks it visited.The source heard it first.—
if current == dstStops at the first time dst leaves the queue.Reached the person.—
while current is not None: path.append(current); current = parent[current]Walks back to the source.Who told you? Who told them?—
return path[::-1]Forwards order.Read the chain src → dst.Forgetting it returns dst → src.
parent[neighbour] = currentRemembers the discoverer.Note who told them.Overwriting a parent later would break shortest-ness; the not in parent check prevents it.

Watch it run. Step through 0 → 5. The second player swaps popleft() for pop() on a 5-node ring (0 → 2).

With pop() the newest node is explored first (depth-first), so 2 is first reached the long way round: [0, 4, 3, 2] instead of [0, 1, 2].

Dry run (generated from the same trace as the first player above):

Invariant. Each node's parent was dequeued before it and is one step closer to the source, so following parents from any node gives a shortest path back to src.

Complexity. O(n + m) time, O(n) space (path length ≤ n).

Mistakes this template invites:

  • Not reversing. Walk back, then read forwards.
  • Using a stack. Ripples, not a dive.
  • Returning [] vs None when unreachable. Check the prompt.

Template D · Multi-source BFS

The question it answersDistance from each node to its nearest source (several sources).
What it keepsdist with every source at 0; a queue seeded with all sources.
When it checks for an answerSame as A.
Use it whenRotting oranges (LC 994), 01 matrix (LC 542), walls and gates, nearest hospital/exit.
Not forOne source (A).
Memory hook: "Drop all the stones at once"Throw several stones into the pond at the same moment. Their ripples spread together; each spot is reached first by the ripple from its nearest stone.

The story, mapped to the code. Several stones, one pond.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
All stones land togetherfor s in sources: dist[s] = 0; queue.append(s)Seed every source at distance 0.
Ripples spread togetherthe A loopUnchanged.
First ripple to arrive winsif neighbour not in distNearest source.

The template. A with a different starting line.

from collections import deque

def multi_source_bfs(graph, sources):
    dist = {s: 0 for s in sources}
    queue = deque(sources)
    while queue:
        current = queue.popleft()
        for neighbour in graph[current]:
            if neighbour not in dist:
                dist[neighbour] = dist[current] + 1
                queue.append(neighbour)
    return dist
function multiSourceBfs(graph: number[][], sources: number[]): Map<number, number> {
  const dist = new Map<number, number>(sources.map((s) => [s, 0]));
  const queue = [...sources];
  for (let head = 0; head < queue.length; head++) {
    const current = queue[head];
    for (const neighbour of graph[current]) {
      if (!dist.has(neighbour)) {
        dist.set(neighbour, dist.get(current)! + 1);
        queue.push(neighbour);
      }
    }
  }
  return dist;
}
static Map<Integer, Integer> multiSourceBfs(List<List<Integer>> graph, List<Integer> sources) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> dist = new HashMap<>();
    for (int s : sources) dist.put(s, 0);
    Deque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(sources);
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int current = queue.poll();
        for (int neighbour : graph.get(current)) {
            if (!dist.containsKey(neighbour)) {
                dist.put(neighbour, dist.get(current) + 1);
                queue.offer(neighbour);
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

6. How to remember it forever

Memory hook: "Ripples in a queue"BFS = ripples spreading out from a pebble. The queue is the line of ripples waiting to spread. Mark when you enqueue ("ticket stamped at the door"), or the same node gets in line many times.
How this hook works: what “Ripples in a queue” means

What the slogan means, phrase by phrase

“Ripples”
BFS spreads out in rings from the start: everything 1 step away, then everything 2 steps away, and so on.
“in a queue”
The queue holds the edge of the ripple. First in, first out, so nearer nodes are always processed before farther ones.
“Mark when you enqueue”
Stamp a node's ticket as it joins the queue (dist[neighbour] = …), not when it leaves. Otherwise the same node can join the line many times.

Why this picture fits the pattern: BFS answers "fewest steps" questions in unweighted graphs. A ripple reaches every point by the shortest route first, because it never skips ahead.

The story → the code

In the storyIn the code
The pebblesrc, dist[src] = 0
Ring numberdist[node]
The ripple's frontqueue (a deque)
Spread one pointcurrent = queue.popleft(), push unseen neighbours
Ticket stamped at the doorset dist[neighbour] when appending
Several pebbles at onceall sources in the queue at distance 0

Watch it on numbers

Graph: 0–1, 0–2, 1–3, 2–3, 3–4. Pebble at 0.

  1. Ring 0: {0}. Spread 0: stamp 1 and 2 at distance 1.
  2. Spread 1: stamp 3 at distance 2. Spread 2: 3 is already stamped, so it doesn't join twice.
  3. Spread 3: stamp 4 at distance 3.
  4. dist = {0: 0, 1: 1, 2: 1, 3: 2, 4: 3}. Each ring is reached by the shortest route.

The trap it saves you from

Marking when you pop instead of when you push: node 3 would be queued by both 1 and 2. On big grids that duplication explodes. Also don't use BFS on weighted edges, which need Dijkstra.

It still works when…

Rotting Oranges: every rotten orange is a pebble dropped at once, and the minutes are the ring numbers. Freeze len(queue) at the start of each round to process exactly one ring.

Picture

Concentric rings around the start, numbered 0, 1, 2, … The ring number is the distance. The queue only ever holds two neighbouring rings at a time.

Chant

"Seed, pop left, stamp and push right. Freeze the size for levels. All sources go in at zero."

DFS vs BFS

"Stack dives, queue ripples." Swap the stack for a queue and a deep explorer becomes a shortest-path finder.

7. LeetCode problems, solved step by step

New to this pattern? Start with theseSolve 637. Average of Levels in Binary Tree, then 111. Minimum Depth of Binary Tree, then 994. Rotting Oranges. They are marked Start here below. Read the explanation, press Play on the step-through, then close the page and solve it yourself on LeetCode.
Medium 994. Rotting Oranges Start here Google Meta Amazon Microsoft MatrixQueue

Problem: A grid holds 0 (empty), 1 (fresh orange) and 2 (rotten orange). Every minute, each rotten orange rots its 4-directional fresh neighbours. Return the minutes until no fresh orange is left, or -1 if some can never rot.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: grid = [[2,1,1],[1,1,0],[0,1,1]]
Output: 4
Example 2
Input: grid = [[2,1,1],[0,1,1],[1,0,1]]
Output: -1
Explanation: The orange in the bottom left corner (row 2, column 0) is never rotten, because rotting only happens 4-directionally.

Constraints: m == grid.length · n == grid[i].length · 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 10 · grid[i][j] is 0, 1, or 2.

Hint 1

All rotten oranges spread at the same time. That's BFS from many starting points at once.

Hint 2

Put every rotten orange in the queue first; each BFS level is one minute. At the end, any fresh orange left means −1.

From brute force to the pattern: Simulating minute by minute by rescanning the whole grid is O((r · c)²). A multi-source BFS spreads from all rotten oranges together and touches each cell once: O(r · c).

Spot it: "every minute, spreads to adjacent" with many starting rotten oranges = multi-source, level-by-level BFS.

Key insight: Put all rotten oranges in the queue at minute 0. Each frozen-size round is one minute. Count the fresh oranges up front so you can tell at the end whether any were unreachable.

Approach:

  1. Scan the grid once. Push every rotten orange into the queue and count the fresh ones.
  2. While the queue is non-empty and fresh oranges remain, process one level (frozen size). That's one minute.
  3. For each popped cell, rot every fresh 4-neighbour: set it to 2 (mark on enqueue), decrease fresh, and enqueue it.
  4. After each level, add 1 to minutes.
  5. Return minutes if fresh == 0, else -1.
class Solution:
    def orangesRotting(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        rows = len(grid)
        cols = len(grid[0])
        # The queue holds (row, col) of rotten oranges that will spread next.
        # append(x) adds at the back, popleft() takes from the front.
        queue = deque()
        fresh = 0
        # Step 1: scan the grid once. Every rotten orange is a starting point,
        # and we count the fresh ones so we know when we are finished.
        for row in range(rows):
            for col in range(cols):
                if grid[row][col] == 2:
                    queue.append((row, col))
                elif grid[row][col] == 1:
                    fresh = fresh + 1
        # The 4 moves as (row change, col change): down, up, right, left.
        directions = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]
        minutes = 0
        # Step 2: go on while something can still spread AND something is still fresh.
        while len(queue) > 0 and fresh > 0:
            # Freeze the size: these are exactly the oranges that spread THIS minute.
            level_size = len(queue)
            for _ in range(level_size):
                cell = queue.popleft()
                row = cell[0]
                col = cell[1]
                for direction in directions:
                    new_row = row + direction[0]
                    new_col = col + direction[1]
                    # Skip cells outside the grid.
                    if new_row < 0 or new_row >= rows or new_col < 0 or new_col >= cols:
                        continue
                    if grid[new_row][new_col] == 1:
                        grid[new_row][new_col] = 2    # rot it now = mark when enqueued
                        fresh = fresh - 1
                        queue.append((new_row, new_col))
            # One whole level is done, so one minute has passed.
            minutes = minutes + 1
        # Step 3: a fresh orange that is left over could never be reached.
        if fresh == 0:
            return minutes
        else:
            return -1

    const rows = grid.length;
    const cols = grid[0].length;
    // The queue holds [row, col] of rotten oranges that will spread next.
    // push(x) adds at the back, shift() takes from the front.
    let queue: [number, number][] = [];
    let fresh = 0;
    // Step 1: scan the grid once. Every rotten orange is a starting point,
    // and we count the fresh ones so we know when we are finished.
    for (let row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
        for (let col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
            if (grid[row][col] === 2) {
                queue.push([row, col]);
            } else if (grid[row][col] === 1) {
                fresh = fresh + 1;

        }
    }

    const directions = [[1, 0], [-1, 0], [0, 1], [0, -1]];
    let minutes = 0;
    // Step 2: go on while something can still spread AND something is still fresh.
    while (queue.length > 0 && fresh > 0) {
        // Freeze the size: these are exactly the oranges that spread THIS minute.
        const levelSize = queue.length;
        for (let k = 0; k < levelSize; k++) {
            const cell = queue.shift()!;
            const row = cell[0];
            const col = cell[1];
            for (const direction of directions) {
                const newRow = row + direction[0];
                const newCol = col + direction[1];
                // Skip cells outside the grid.
                if (newRow < 0 || newRow >= rows || newCol < 0 || newCol >= cols) {
                    continue;
                }
                if (grid[newRow][newCol] === 1) {
                    grid[newRow][newCol] = 2;  // rot it now = mark when enqueued
                    fresh = fresh - 1;
                    queue.push([newRow, newCol]);
                }
            }
        }
        // One whole level is done, so one minute has passed.
        minutes = minutes + 1;
    }
    // Step 3: a fresh orange that is left over could never be reached.
    if (fresh === 0) {
        return minutes;
    } else {
        return -1;
    }

class Solution {
    public int orangesRotting(int[][] grid) {
        int rows = grid.length;
        int cols = grid[0].length;
        // The queue holds (row, col) of rotten oranges that will spread next.
        // offer(x) adds at the back, poll() takes from the front.
        Deque<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int fresh = 0;
        // Step 1: scan the grid once. Every rotten orange is a starting point,
        // and we count the fresh ones so we know when we are finished.
        for (int row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
            for (int col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
                if (grid[row][col] == 2) {
                    queue.offer(new int[] {row, col});
                } else if (grid[row][col] == 1) {
                    fresh = fresh + 1;
                }
            }
        }
        // The 4 moves as (row change, col change): down, up, right, left.
        int[][] directions = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
        int minutes = 0;
        // Step 2: go on while something can still spread AND something is still fresh.
        while (queue.size() > 0 && fresh > 0) {
            // Freeze the size: these are exactly the oranges that spread THIS minute.
            int levelSize = queue.size();
            for (int k = 0; k < levelSize; k++) {
                int[] cell = queue.poll();
                int row = cell[0];
                int col = cell[1];
                for (int[] direction : directions) {
                    int newRow = row + direction[0];
                    int newCol = col + direction[1];
                    // Skip cells outside the grid.
                    if (newRow < 0 || newRow >= rows || newCol < 0 || newCol >= cols) {
                        continue;
                    }
                    if (grid[newRow][newCol] == 1) {
                        grid[newRow][newCol] = 2;  // rot it now = mark when enqueued
                        fresh = fresh - 1;
                        queue.offer(new int[] {newRow, newCol});
                    }
                }
            }
            // One whole level is done, so one minute has passed.
            minutes = minutes + 1;
        }
        // Step 3: a fresh orange that is left over could never be reached.
        if (fresh == 0) {
            return minutes;
        } else {
            return -1;
        }
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. rows and cols store the grid size so the bounds checks are easy to read.
  2. Step 1 (scan): the double for loop visits every cell. Rotten cells (2) go into the queue as (row, col) pairs; fresh cells (1) are only counted in fresh.
  3. directions lists the 4 moves as (row change, col change). Adding one to a cell's position gives a neighbour.
  4. Step 2 (spread): the while loop runs while there are rotten oranges to spread from and fresh oranges left to rot. The second condition stops us counting an extra empty minute at the end.
  5. level_size = len(queue) freezes this minute's rotten oranges. Each one is popped and split into row and col by indexing (cell[0], cell[1]).
  6. For each direction, out-of-grid neighbours are skipped with continue. A fresh neighbour is set to 2 straight away (so nobody rots it twice), fresh goes down by 1, and it is queued for the next minute.
  7. After the whole level, minutes goes up by 1.
  8. Step 3: if fresh reached 0, return the minutes; otherwise some orange was walled off, so return -1.

Edge cases to test:

  • No fresh oranges at the start → 0.
  • A fresh orange that can never be reached → −1.
  • No rotten oranges but some fresh ones → −1.

Complexity: O(R·C) time and space.

Medium 752. Open the Lock Amazon Microsoft StringQueueHash Set

Problem: A 4-wheel lock starts at "0000". One move turns one wheel up or down by one (9 wraps to 0). Avoid every code in deadends. Return the minimum number of moves to reach target, or -1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: deadends = ["0201","0101","0102","1212","2002"], target = "0202"
Output: 6
Explanation: A sequence of valid moves would be "0000" -> "1000" -> "1100" -> "1200" -> "1201" -> "1202" -> "0202". Note that a sequence like "0000" -> "0001" -> "0002" -> "0102" -> "0202" would be invalid, because the wheels of the lock become stuck after the display becomes the dead end "0102".
Example 2
Input: deadends = ["8888"], target = "0009"
Output: 1
Explanation: We can turn the last wheel in reverse to move from "0000" -> "0009".

Constraints: 1 ≤ deadends.length ≤ 500 · deadends[i].length == 4 · target.length == 4 · target will not be in the list deadends. · target and deadends[i] consist of digits only.

Hint 1

Each lock state is a node; turning one wheel by one notch is an edge.

Hint 2

BFS from "0000", skipping dead ends and visited states; each level is one more move.

From brute force to the pattern: DFS over all combinations doesn't find the minimum number of moves. BFS over the 10,000 states, each with 8 neighbours, finds it in O(10⁴ · 8).

Spot it: "minimum number of turns", and each turn costs 1. The graph is implicit: nodes are the 104 codes, and every code has 8 neighbours.

Key insight: Generate neighbours on the fly and treat deadends as pre-visited walls. Check whether "0000" itself is a deadend.

Approach:

  1. Put the deadends in a set. If "0000" is a deadend, return -1.
  2. BFS from ("0000", 0) with a seen set.
  3. Pop a code. If it's the target, return the number of turns.
  4. Generate its 8 neighbours (each of 4 wheels, ±1 with wrap-around), and enqueue the ones not seen and not dead.
  5. If the queue empties, return -1.
class Solution:
    def openLock(self, deadends: List[str], target: str) -> int:
        # A set makes "is this code a deadend?" an instant check.
        dead = set(deadends)
        if "0000" in dead:
            return -1               # stuck before the first move
        seen = set()
        seen.add("0000")
        # The queue holds (code, turns used to reach it).
        # append(x) adds at the back, popleft() takes from the front.
        queue = deque()
        queue.append(("0000", 0))
        while len(queue) > 0:
            pair = queue.popleft()
            code = pair[0]
            turns = pair[1]
            if code == target:
                return turns        # first time we pop the target = fewest turns
            # Build the 8 neighbours: each of the 4 wheels turned up (+1) or down (-1).
            for i in range(4):
                digit = int(code[i])
                for step in [1, -1]:
                    # % 10 wraps around: 9 + 1 becomes 0, and 0 - 1 becomes 9.
                    new_digit = (digit + step) % 10
                    next_code = code[:i] + str(new_digit) + code[i + 1:]
                    if next_code not in seen and next_code not in dead:
                        seen.add(next_code)        # mark when enqueued
                        queue.append((next_code, turns + 1))
        # Every reachable code was tried and none was the target.
        return -1
function openLock(deadends: string[], target: string): number {
    // A set makes "is this code a deadend?" an instant check.
    const dead = new Set(deadends);
    if (dead.has("0000")) {
        return -1;  // stuck before the first move
    }
    const seen = new Set<string>();
    seen.add("0000");
    // The queue holds [code, turns used to reach it].
    // push(x) adds at the back; head moves forward instead of shift(), which is O(n).
    const queue: [string, number][] = [];
    queue.push(["0000", 0]);
    let head = 0;
    while (head < queue.length) {
        const pair = queue[head++];
        const code = pair[0];
        const turns = pair[1];
        if (code === target) {
            return turns;  // first time we pop the target = fewest turns
        }
        // Build the 8 neighbours: each of the 4 wheels turned up (+1) or down (-1).
        for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
            const digit = Number(code[i]);
            for (const step of [1, -1]) {
                // + 10 then % 10 wraps around: 9 + 1 becomes 0, and 0 - 1 becomes 9.
                const newDigit = (digit + step + 10) % 10;
                const nextCode = code.slice(0, i) + String(newDigit) + code.slice(i + 1);
                if (!seen.has(nextCode) && !dead.has(nextCode)) {
                    seen.add(nextCode);  // mark when enqueued
                    queue.push([nextCode, turns + 1]);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    // Every reachable code was tried and none was the target.
    return -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int openLock(String[] deadends, String target) {
        // A set makes "is this code a deadend?" an instant check.
        Set<String> dead = new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList(deadends));
        if (dead.contains("0000")) {
            return -1;  // stuck before the first move
        }
        Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
        seen.add("0000");
        // The queue holds (code, turns used to reach it).
        // offer(x) adds at the back, poll() takes from the front.
        Deque<Object[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.offer(new Object[] {"0000", 0});
        while (queue.size() > 0) {
            Object[] pair = queue.poll();
            String code = (String) pair[0];
            int turns = (Integer) pair[1];
            if (code.equals(target)) {
                return turns;  // first time we pop the target = fewest turns
            }
            // Build the 8 neighbours: each of the 4 wheels turned up (+1) or down (-1).
            for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
                int digit = code.charAt(i) - '0';
                for (int step : new int[] {1, -1}) {
                    // + 10 then % 10 wraps around: 9 + 1 becomes 0, and 0 - 1 becomes 9.
                    int newDigit = (digit + step + 10) % 10;
                    String nextCode = code.substring(0, i) + newDigit + code.substring(i + 1);
                    if (!seen.contains(nextCode) && !dead.contains(nextCode)) {
                        seen.add(nextCode);  // mark when enqueued
                        queue.offer(new Object[] {nextCode, turns + 1});
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        // Every reachable code was tried and none was the target.
        return -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. dead = set(deadends) turns the list into a set, so "is this a deadend?" takes constant time.
  2. If "0000" itself is dead we can't move at all, so return -1.
  3. The queue holds pairs (code, turns). Each pop is split by indexing: pair[0] is the code, pair[1] the number of turns used.
  4. If the popped code is the target, BFS guarantees turns is the minimum, so return it.
  5. Otherwise build the 8 neighbours. For each wheel i (0 to 3) and each step (+1 or -1), (digit + step) % 10 gives the new digit with wrap-around, and code[:i] + str(new_digit) + code[i + 1:] glues the string back together with that one digit changed.
  6. A neighbour that is neither seen nor dead is marked seen and queued with turns + 1.
  7. If the queue empties, the target can't be reached: return -1.

Dry run on deadends = ["0201","0101","0102","1212","2002"], target = "0202" (answer 6). The queue gets large, so this table counts codes per BFS level:

turnsCodes popped at this levelNotes
01"0000"
18"1000", "9000", "0100", "0900", "0010", "0090", "0001", "0009"
23132 codes are 2 turns away, but deadend "0101" is never queued
386
4190
5356
6150the 150th code popped at this level is "0202" → return 6

Every 4-turn route (like "0000" → "0100" → "0200" → "0201" → "0202") passes through a deadend ("0101", "0201" or "0102"), which is why the answer is 6 turns instead of 4.

Edge cases to test:

  • "0000" itself is a dead end → −1.
  • The target is "0000" → 0.
  • Wrap-around between 9 and 0.

Complexity: O(104 · 8 · 4) time, i.e. constant for this fixed lock; O(104) space.

Medium 310. Minimum Height Trees Google Amazon Microsoft GraphQueue

Problem: Given a tree of n nodes (as undirected edges), return every node that, when chosen as the root, gives the minimum possible height.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 4, edges = [[1,0],[1,2],[1,3]]
Output: [1]
Explanation: As shown, the height of the tree is 1 when the root is the node with label 1 which is the only MHT.
Example 2
Input: n = 6, edges = [[3,0],[3,1],[3,2],[3,4],[5,4]]
Output: [3,4]

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 2 * 10⁴ · edges.length == n - 1 · 0 ≤ ai, bi < n · ai != bi · All the pairs (ai, bi) are distinct. · The given input is guaranteed to be a tree and there will be no repeated edges.

Hint 1

The best roots are in the "middle" of the tree.

Hint 2

Peel off leaves layer by layer (BFS on degrees); the last 1 or 2 nodes left are the answer.

From brute force to the pattern: Running a BFS from every node to measure its height is O(n²). Trimming leaves inward, like a topological sort, finds the centre in O(n).

Spot it: Running a BFS from every node is O(n²). The best roots are the centre of the tree, and you can find the centre with a BFS that runs from the outside in.

Key insight: Multi-source BFS starting from all leaves. Peel off one layer of leaves per round. Nodes whose degree drops to 1 become the next layer. When 2 or fewer nodes remain, those are the centres (a tree has one or two of them).

Approach:

  1. If n <= 2, every node is a centre.
  2. Build adjacency sets (removal is easy) and put every leaf (degree 1) in a queue.
  3. While more than 2 nodes remain, subtract the number of leaves in this layer, then remove each one.
  4. Removing a leaf detaches it from its only neighbour. If that neighbour's degree drops to 1, it joins the next layer.
  5. The 1 or 2 nodes left at the end are the answer.
class Solution:
    def findMinHeightTrees(self, n: int, edges: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        # With 1 or 2 nodes, every node is a centre.
        if n <= 2:
            answer = []
            for node in range(n):
                answer.append(node)
            return answer
        # graph[node] = set of its neighbours. A set makes removing one easy.
        graph = {}
        for node in range(n):
            graph[node] = set()
        for edge in edges:
            first = edge[0]
            second = edge[1]
            graph[first].add(second)
            graph[second].add(first)
        # The outer layer = every leaf (a node with exactly one neighbour).
        # append(x) adds at the back, popleft() takes from the front.
        leaves = deque()
        for node in range(n):
            if len(graph[node]) == 1:
                leaves.append(node)
        remaining = n
        # Peel one layer of leaves per round until only 1 or 2 nodes are left.
        while remaining > 2:
            layer_size = len(leaves)
            remaining = remaining - layer_size
            for _ in range(layer_size):
                leaf = leaves.popleft()
                # A leaf has exactly one neighbour. pop() takes it out of the set.
                neighbour = graph[leaf].pop()
                # Remove the edge from the neighbour's side too.
                graph[neighbour].remove(leaf)
                if len(graph[neighbour]) == 1:
                    # The neighbour has just become a leaf: it belongs to the next layer.
                    leaves.append(neighbour)
        # The nodes still in the queue are the centres.
        answer = []
        for node in leaves:
            answer.append(node)
        answer.sort()               # any order is accepted; sorted is easier to read
        return answer
function findMinHeightTrees(n: number, edges: number[][]): number[] {
    // With 1 or 2 nodes, every node is a centre.
    if (n <= 2) {
        const answer: number[] = [];
        for (let node = 0; node < n; node++) {
            answer.push(node);
        }
        return answer;
    }
    // graph[node] = set of its neighbours. A set makes removing one easy.
    const graph: Set<number>[] = [];
    for (let node = 0; node < n; node++) {
        graph.push(new Set());
    }
    for (const edge of edges) {
        const first = edge[0];
        const second = edge[1];
        graph[first].add(second);
        graph[second].add(first);
    }
    // The outer layer = every leaf (a node with exactly one neighbour).
    // push(x) adds at the back, shift() takes from the front.
    const leaves: number[] = [];
    for (let node = 0; node < n; node++) {
        if (graph[node].size === 1) {
            leaves.push(node);
        }
    }
    let remaining = n;
    // Peel one layer of leaves per round until only 1 or 2 nodes are left.
    while (remaining > 2) {
        const layerSize = leaves.length;
        remaining = remaining - layerSize;
        for (let k = 0; k < layerSize; k++) {
            const leaf = leaves.shift()!;
            // A leaf has exactly one neighbour: take it out of the set.
            const neighbour = graph[leaf].values().next().value!;
            graph[leaf].delete(neighbour);
            // Remove the edge from the neighbour's side too.
            graph[neighbour].delete(leaf);
            if (graph[neighbour].size === 1) {
                // The neighbour has just become a leaf: it belongs to the next layer.
                leaves.push(neighbour);
            }
        }
    }
    // The nodes still in the queue are the centres.
    const answer: number[] = [];
    for (const node of leaves) {
        answer.push(node);
    }
    answer.sort((a, b) => a - b);  // any order is accepted; sorted is easier to read
    return answer;
}
class Solution {
    public List<Integer> findMinHeightTrees(int n, int[][] edges) {
        // With 1 or 2 nodes, every node is a centre.
        if (n <= 2) {
            List<Integer> answer = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) {
                answer.add(node);
            }
            return answer;
        }
        // graph.get(node) = set of its neighbours. A set makes removing one easy.
        List<Set<Integer>> graph = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) {
            graph.add(new HashSet<>());
        }
        for (int[] edge : edges) {
            int first = edge[0];
            int second = edge[1];
            graph.get(first).add(second);
            graph.get(second).add(first);
        }
        // The outer layer = every leaf (a node with exactly one neighbour).
        // offer(x) adds at the back, poll() takes from the front.
        Deque<Integer> leaves = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) {
            if (graph.get(node).size() == 1) {
                leaves.offer(node);
            }
        }
        int remaining = n;
        // Peel one layer of leaves per round until only 1 or 2 nodes are left.
        while (remaining > 2) {
            int layerSize = leaves.size();
            remaining = remaining - layerSize;
            for (int k = 0; k < layerSize; k++) {
                int leaf = leaves.poll();
                // A leaf has exactly one neighbour: take it out of the set.
                int neighbour = graph.get(leaf).iterator().next();
                graph.get(leaf).remove(neighbour);
                // Remove the edge from the neighbour's side too.
                graph.get(neighbour).remove(leaf);
                if (graph.get(neighbour).size() == 1) {
                    // The neighbour has just become a leaf: it belongs to the next layer.
                    leaves.offer(neighbour);
                }
            }
        }
        // The nodes still in the queue are the centres.
        List<Integer> answer = new ArrayList<>(leaves);
        Collections.sort(answer);  // any order is accepted; sorted is easier to read
        return answer;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. With 1 or 2 nodes, every node is a centre, so we return [0] or [0, 1], built with a loop.
  2. graph maps each node to a set of neighbours. Every edge [first, second] is added both ways because the tree is undirected.
  3. The first leaves queue holds every node with exactly one neighbour: the outer layer of the tree.
  4. remaining counts nodes not yet peeled. While more than 2 remain, we take a whole layer: layer_size is frozen and subtracted from remaining.
  5. For each leaf, graph[leaf].pop() removes and returns its only neighbour, and graph[neighbour].remove(leaf) removes the edge from the other side.
  6. If the neighbour is down to one neighbour, it has become a leaf of the smaller tree, so it joins the queue for the next layer.
  7. When 2 or fewer nodes remain, the queue holds exactly those centres. We copy them into a list and sort it.

Dry run on n = 6, edges = [[3,0],[3,1],[3,2],[3,4],[5,4]] (answer [3, 4]). Node 3 has neighbours {0, 1, 2, 4}; node 4 has {3, 5}.

Roundremaining (before → after)Leaf poppedIts neighbour's degree afterleaves queue
(start)6--[0, 1, 2, 5]
16 → 203 has 3 left[1, 2, 5]
113 has 2 left[2, 5]
123 has 1 left → queued[5, 3]
154 has 1 left → queued[3, 4]

remaining = 2, so the loop stops and the answer is [3, 4].

Edge cases to test:

  • n = 1 → [0].
  • n = 2 → [0, 1].
  • A star-shaped tree → the centre node.

Complexity: O(n) time and space.

Hard 127. Word Ladder Google Meta Amazon Cisco Apple StringGraphQueueHash Set

Problem: Transform beginWord into endWord by changing one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in wordList. Return the number of words in the shortest sequence (including both ends), or 0.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: beginWord = "hit", endWord = "cog", wordList = ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log","cog"]
Output: 5
Explanation: One shortest transformation sequence is "hit" -> "hot" -> "dot" -> "dog" -> cog", which is 5 words long.
Example 2
Input: beginWord = "hit", endWord = "cog", wordList = ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log"]
Output: 0
Explanation: The endWord "cog" is not in wordList, therefore there is no valid transformation sequence.

Constraints: 1 ≤ beginWord.length ≤ 10 · endWord.length == beginWord.length · 1 ≤ wordList.length ≤ 5000 · wordList[i].length == beginWord.length · beginWord, endWord, and wordList[i] consist of lowercase English letters. · beginWord != endWord · All the words in wordList are unique.

Hint 1

Words are nodes; two words are connected if they differ by exactly one letter. You want the shortest path.

Hint 2

BFS from beginWord. To find neighbours fast, try each position × each letter, or group words by patterns like h*t.

From brute force to the pattern: Comparing every pair of words to build the graph is O(n² · L). Generating neighbours with wildcard patterns plus BFS finds the shortest chain in O(n · L²).

Spot it: "shortest transformation sequence" + "one letter at a time" = BFS on an implicit graph of words.

Key insight: Comparing every pair of words is slow. Instead, bucket words by wildcard patterns: hot belongs to *ot, h*t, ho*. Two words are neighbours if they share a bucket. Empty each bucket after its first use, because later visits can't produce a shorter path.

Approach:

  1. If endWord isn't in the word list, return 0.
  2. Bucket every word by its wildcard patterns, e.g. hot → *ot, h*t, ho*.
  3. BFS from (beginWord, 1). Pop a word and return its step count if it's endWord.
  4. For each of its patterns, enqueue every unseen word in that bucket with steps + 1, then empty the bucket.
  5. If the queue empties, return 0.
class Solution:
    def ladderLength(self, beginWord: str, endWord: str, wordList: List[str]) -> int:
        words = set(wordList)
        if endWord not in words:
            return 0
        # buckets["h*t"] = every word that fits h?t, for example ["hot", "hit"].
        # Two words in the same bucket differ in exactly one letter.
        all_words = []
        for word in wordList:
            all_words.append(word)
        if beginWord not in words:
            all_words.append(beginWord)
        buckets = {}
        for word in all_words:
            for i in range(len(word)):
                pattern = word[:i] + "*" + word[i + 1:]
                if pattern not in buckets:
                    buckets[pattern] = []
                buckets[pattern].append(word)
        seen = set()
        seen.add(beginWord)
        # The queue holds (word, number of words in the sequence so far).
        # append(x) adds at the back, popleft() takes from the front.
        queue = deque()
        queue.append((beginWord, 1))
        while len(queue) > 0:
            pair = queue.popleft()
            word = pair[0]
            steps = pair[1]
            if word == endWord:
                return steps
            for i in range(len(word)):
                pattern = word[:i] + "*" + word[i + 1:]
                for next_word in buckets[pattern]:
                    if next_word not in seen:
                        seen.add(next_word)
                        queue.append((next_word, steps + 1))
                # Empty the bucket: all its words are queued now, a later visit can't help.
                buckets[pattern] = []
        return 0
function ladderLength(beginWord: string, endWord: string, wordList: string[]): number {
    const words = new Set(wordList);
    if (!words.has(endWord)) {
        return 0;
    }
    // buckets.get("h*t") = every word that fits h?t, for example ["hot", "hit"].
    // Two words in the same bucket differ in exactly one letter.
    const allWords: string[] = [];
    for (const word of wordList) {
        allWords.push(word);
    }
    if (!words.has(beginWord)) {
        allWords.push(beginWord);
    }
    const buckets = new Map<string, string[]>();
    for (const word of allWords) {
        for (let i = 0; i < word.length; i++) {
            const pattern = word.slice(0, i) + "*" + word.slice(i + 1);
            if (!buckets.has(pattern)) {
                buckets.set(pattern, []);
            }
            buckets.get(pattern)!.push(word);
        }
    }
    const seen = new Set<string>();
    seen.add(beginWord);
    // The queue holds [word, number of words in the sequence so far].
    // push(x) adds at the back; head moves forward instead of shift(), which is O(n).
    const queue: [string, number][] = [];
    queue.push([beginWord, 1]);
    let head = 0;
    while (head < queue.length) {
        const pair = queue[head++];
        const word = pair[0];
        const steps = pair[1];
        if (word === endWord) {
            return steps;
        }
        for (let i = 0; i < word.length; i++) {
            const pattern = word.slice(0, i) + "*" + word.slice(i + 1);
            for (const nextWord of buckets.get(pattern)!) {
                if (!seen.has(nextWord)) {
                    seen.add(nextWord);
                    queue.push([nextWord, steps + 1]);
                }
            }
            // Empty the bucket: all its words are queued now, a later visit can't help.
            buckets.set(pattern, []);
        }
    }
    return 0;
}
class Solution {
    public int ladderLength(String beginWord, String endWord, List<String> wordList) {
        Set<String> words = new HashSet<>(wordList);
        if (!words.contains(endWord)) {
            return 0;
        }
        // buckets.get("h*t") = every word that fits h?t, for example ["hot", "hit"].
        // Two words in the same bucket differ in exactly one letter.
        List<String> allWords = new ArrayList<>(wordList);
        if (!words.contains(beginWord)) {
            allWords.add(beginWord);
        }
        Map<String, List<String>> buckets = new HashMap<>();
        for (String word : allWords) {
            for (int i = 0; i < word.length(); i++) {
                String pattern = word.substring(0, i) + "*" + word.substring(i + 1);
                buckets.computeIfAbsent(pattern, key -> new ArrayList<>()).add(word);
            }
        }
        Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
        seen.add(beginWord);
        // The queue holds (word, number of words in the sequence so far).
        // offer(x) adds at the back, poll() takes from the front.
        Deque<Object[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.offer(new Object[] {beginWord, 1});
        while (queue.size() > 0) {
            Object[] pair = queue.poll();
            String word = (String) pair[0];
            int steps = (Integer) pair[1];
            if (word.equals(endWord)) {
                return steps;
            }
            for (int i = 0; i < word.length(); i++) {
                String pattern = word.substring(0, i) + "*" + word.substring(i + 1);
                for (String nextWord : buckets.get(pattern)) {
                    if (!seen.contains(nextWord)) {
                        seen.add(nextWord);
                        queue.offer(new Object[] {nextWord, steps + 1});
                    }
                }
                // Empty the bucket: all its words are queued now, a later visit can't help.
                buckets.put(pattern, new ArrayList<>());
            }
        }
        return 0;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. If endWord isn't in the word list, no sequence can end there: return 0.
  2. all_words is the word list plus beginWord (if it isn't already in it).
  3. For every word and every position i, word[:i] + "*" + word[i + 1:] replaces letter i with *. That pattern is the bucket key. If the key is new, we create an empty list first, then add the word.
  4. BFS starts at (beginWord, 1), because the answer counts words, and the first word counts as 1.
  5. Each pop is split into word = pair[0] and steps = pair[1]. If it's endWord, return steps.
  6. For each of the word's patterns, every unseen word in that bucket is one letter away: mark it and queue it with steps + 1.
  7. buckets[pattern] = [] empties the bucket. Everything in it is already queued, so looking at it again later would be wasted work.

Dry run on beginWord = "hit", endWord = "cog", wordList = ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log","cog"] (answer 5):

Pop (word, steps)Buckets that give new wordsQueuedQueue after this word
("hit", 1)"h*t" = [hot, hit]hot[(hot, 2)]
("hot", 2)"*ot" = [hot, dot, lot]dot, lot[(dot, 3), (lot, 3)]
("dot", 3)"do*" = [dot, dog]dog[(lot, 3), (dog, 4)]
("lot", 3)"lo*" = [lot, log]log[(dog, 4), (log, 4)]
("dog", 4)"*og" = [dog, log, cog]cog[(log, 4), (cog, 5)]
("log", 4)none ("*og" already emptied)-[(cog, 5)]
("cog", 5)it's endWord → return 5 (hit → hot → dot → dog → cog)

Edge cases to test:

  • endWord not in the list → 0.
  • beginWord one step from endWord → 2.
  • Disconnected words → 0.

Complexity: O(N · L²) time (N words of length L, building the strings), O(N · L²) space. Bidirectional BFS (from both ends) speeds it up further in practice.

Hard 815. Bus Routes Google Amazon ArrayGraphQueue

Problem: routes[i] is the loop of stops bus i visits. Starting at stop source, what's the fewest number of buses you must take to reach target? Return -1 if it's impossible.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: routes = [[1,2,7],[3,6,7]], source = 1, target = 6
Output: 2
Explanation: The best strategy is take the first bus to the bus stop 7, then take the second bus to the bus stop 6.
Example 2
Input: routes = [[7,12],[4,5,15],[6],[15,19],[9,12,13]], source = 15, target = 12
Output: -1

Constraints: 1 ≤ routes.length ≤ 500. · 1 ≤ routes[i].length ≤ 10⁵ · All the values of routes[i] are unique. · sum(routes[i].length) ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ routes[i][j] < 10⁶ · 0 ≤ source, target < 10⁶

Hint 1

Count buses, not stops. Which stops connect one bus to another?

Hint 2

BFS where each level boards one more bus: from a stop, take every unused route through it and visit all its stops.

From brute force to the pattern: BFS over stops, one stop per step, counts stops instead of buses and is slow. BFS by routes, marking each route as used once, gives the minimum number of buses in O(total stops).

Spot it: "fewest buses" = BFS, but the cost is per bus, not per stop. Each BFS level must be "one more bus".

Key insight: Expand a whole bus at once. From a stop, every unused bus through it reaches all of that bus's stops at cost +1. Mark buses as used so each route is expanded only once. Otherwise long routes make it O(stops²).

Approach:

  1. If source == target, return 0.
  2. Map each stop to the buses that serve it.
  3. BFS over (stop, buses_taken), starting at (source, 0).
  4. From a stop, take every bus not used yet: mark it used, and reach all of its stops at buses + 1.
  5. Return as soon as one of those stops is the target. If the queue empties, return -1.
class Solution:
    def numBusesToDestination(self, routes: List[List[int]], source: int, target: int) -> int:
        if source == target:
            return 0
        # stop_to_buses[stop] = list of the bus numbers that visit this stop.
        stop_to_buses = {}
        for bus in range(len(routes)):
            for stop in routes[bus]:
                if stop not in stop_to_buses:
                    stop_to_buses[stop] = []
                stop_to_buses[stop].append(bus)
        used_bus = set()            # buses we have already ridden
        seen_stop = set()           # stops we have already put in the queue
        seen_stop.add(source)
        # The queue holds (stop, buses taken to get here).
        # append(x) adds at the back, popleft() takes from the front.
        queue = deque()
        queue.append((source, 0))
        while len(queue) > 0:
            pair = queue.popleft()
            stop = pair[0]
            buses = pair[1]
            if stop not in stop_to_buses:
                continue            # no bus serves this stop
            for bus in stop_to_buses[stop]:
                if bus in used_bus:
                    continue        # each bus only needs to be ridden once
                used_bus.add(bus)
                # Riding this bus reaches ALL of its stops for one more bus.
                for next_stop in routes[bus]:
                    if next_stop == target:
                        return buses + 1
                    if next_stop not in seen_stop:
                        seen_stop.add(next_stop)
                        queue.append((next_stop, buses + 1))
        return -1
function numBusesToDestination(routes: number[][], source: number, target: number): number {
    if (source === target) {
        return 0;
    }
    // stopToBuses.get(stop) = list of the bus numbers that visit this stop.
    const stopToBuses = new Map<number, number[]>();
    for (let bus = 0; bus < routes.length; bus++) {
        for (const stop of routes[bus]) {
            if (!stopToBuses.has(stop)) {
                stopToBuses.set(stop, []);
            }
            stopToBuses.get(stop)!.push(bus);
        }
    }
    const usedBus = new Set<number>();   // buses we have already ridden
    const seenStop = new Set<number>();  // stops we have already put in the queue
    seenStop.add(source);
    // The queue holds [stop, buses taken to get here].
    // push(x) adds at the back; head moves forward instead of shift(), which is O(n).
    const queue: [number, number][] = [];
    queue.push([source, 0]);
    let head = 0;
    while (head < queue.length) {
        const pair = queue[head++];
        const stop = pair[0];
        const buses = pair[1];
        if (!stopToBuses.has(stop)) {
            continue;  // no bus serves this stop
        }
        for (const bus of stopToBuses.get(stop)!) {
            if (usedBus.has(bus)) {
                continue;  // each bus only needs to be ridden once
            }
            usedBus.add(bus);
            // Riding this bus reaches ALL of its stops for one more bus.
            for (const nextStop of routes[bus]) {
                if (nextStop === target) {
                    return buses + 1;
                }
                if (!seenStop.has(nextStop)) {
                    seenStop.add(nextStop);
                    queue.push([nextStop, buses + 1]);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int numBusesToDestination(int[][] routes, int source, int target) {
        if (source == target) {
            return 0;
        }
        // stopToBuses.get(stop) = list of the bus numbers that visit this stop.
        Map<Integer, List<Integer>> stopToBuses = new HashMap<>();
        for (int bus = 0; bus < routes.length; bus++) {
            for (int stop : routes[bus]) {
                stopToBuses.computeIfAbsent(stop, key -> new ArrayList<>()).add(bus);
            }
        }
        Set<Integer> usedBus = new HashSet<>();   // buses we have already ridden
        Set<Integer> seenStop = new HashSet<>();  // stops we have already put in the queue
        seenStop.add(source);
        // The queue holds (stop, buses taken to get here).
        // offer(x) adds at the back, poll() takes from the front.
        Deque<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.offer(new int[] {source, 0});
        while (queue.size() > 0) {
            int[] pair = queue.poll();
            int stop = pair[0];
            int buses = pair[1];
            if (!stopToBuses.containsKey(stop)) {
                continue;  // no bus serves this stop
            }
            for (int bus : stopToBuses.get(stop)) {
                if (usedBus.contains(bus)) {
                    continue;  // each bus only needs to be ridden once
                }
                usedBus.add(bus);
                // Riding this bus reaches ALL of its stops for one more bus.
                for (int nextStop : routes[bus]) {
                    if (nextStop == target) {
                        return buses + 1;
                    }
                    if (!seenStop.contains(nextStop)) {
                        seenStop.add(nextStop);
                        queue.offer(new int[] {nextStop, buses + 1});
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. If we're already at the target, we need 0 buses.
  2. stop_to_buses is built with two loops: for every bus number and every stop on its route, add the bus to that stop's list (creating the list the first time we see the stop).
  3. used_bus remembers buses we've already ridden; seen_stop remembers stops already queued.
  4. The queue holds (stop, buses). Each pop is split by indexing. A stop no bus visits is skipped.
  5. For each unused bus at this stop, mark it used and walk its whole route. Every stop on it costs buses + 1. If one of them is the target, return right away; otherwise queue new stops.
  6. Marking the bus as used is what keeps this fast: each route is scanned once, however many of its stops we later pop.

Dry run on routes = [[1,2,7],[3,6,7]], source = 1, target = 6 (answer 2). stop_to_buses = {1: [0], 2: [0], 7: [0, 1], 3: [1], 6: [1]}.

Pop (stop, buses)Bus riddenStops reachedQueue after
(1, 0)bus 01 (seen), 2, 7[(2, 1), (7, 1)]
(2, 1)none (bus 0 already used)-[(7, 1)]
(7, 1)bus 1 (bus 0 skipped)3 → queued, 6 = targetreturn 1 + 1 = 2

Edge cases to test:

  • source == target → 0.
  • The target is unreachable → −1.
  • A stop shared by many routes.

Complexity: O(Σ len(routes[i])) time and space: each bus and each stop is expanded once.

8. Common mistakes

Marking visited when popping instead of when pushingThen the same node can be added to the queue many times before it's popped. That still gives correct distances, but it can blow up to exponential time and memory on dense graphs. Mark the moment you append.
Using a list with pop(0)list.pop(0) is O(n). Use collections.deque and popleft(), which is O(1).
Running one BFS per sourceFor "distance to the nearest X", seed every X at once (multi-source). It's k times faster and simpler.
Off-by-one on levelsDecide whether you count edges (moves) or nodes (Word Ladder counts words), and whether to stop the loop when nothing is left to do (Rotting Oranges' while len(queue) > 0 and fresh > 0).
BFS on weighted graphsBFS's "first arrival is shortest" guarantee holds only when every edge costs the same. With weights, use Dijkstra.

9. Self-check quiz

When should a node be marked as seen in BFS?

Marking on enqueue guarantees each node enters the queue at most once, so the total work is O(V + E).

"Fill each empty room with the distance to its nearest gate" (Walls and Gates). Best approach?

Seed every gate at distance 0. The ripples meet in the middle, and each room is reached first by its nearest gate, all in a single O(R·C) pass.

Shortest travel time on a road network where each road has a different length?

Unequal edge weights break BFS's ring order. Dijkstra replaces the FIFO queue with a min-heap keyed by distance.

To process exactly one level per round, the inner loop runs how many times?

Freeze the size before popping. Nodes pushed during the round belong to the next level.

Easy 111. Minimum Depth of Binary Tree Start here Google Amazon Binary TreeQueue

Problem: Return the number of nodes on the shortest path from the root down to a leaf (a node with no children).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: root = [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]
Output: 2
Example 2
Input: root = [2,null,3,null,4,null,5,null,6]
Output: 5

Constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 10⁵]. · -1000 ≤ Node.val ≤ 1000

Hint 1

The minimum depth is the distance to the nearest leaf.

Hint 2

BFS level by level and stop at the first leaf you meet.

From brute force to the pattern: DFS must explore the whole tree to be sure of the minimum; it also has a trap: a node with one child is not a leaf. BFS stops at the shallowest leaf, often without visiting most of the tree.

Spot it: "minimum depth" is the shortest distance. BFS reaches shallow nodes first, so the first leaf it pops is the answer and it can stop early.

Approach:

  1. If the tree is empty, return 0.
  2. BFS with the queue holding (node, depth), starting at (root, 1).
  3. Pop a node. If it has no children, return its depth.
  4. Otherwise enqueue its children with depth + 1.
class Solution:
    def minDepth(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        if root is None:
            return 0
        # The queue holds (node, depth of that node). The root has depth 1.
        # append(x) adds at the back, popleft() takes from the front.
        queue = deque()
        queue.append((root, 1))
        while len(queue) > 0:
            pair = queue.popleft()
            node = pair[0]
            depth = pair[1]
            # A leaf has no children. The first leaf we pop is the shallowest one.
            if node.left is None and node.right is None:
                return depth
            if node.left is not None:
                queue.append((node.left, depth + 1))
            if node.right is not None:
                queue.append((node.right, depth + 1))
        return 0                    # never reached for a non-empty tree
function minDepth(root: TreeNode | null): number {
    if (root === null) {
        return 0;
    }
    // The queue holds [node, depth of that node]. The root has depth 1.
    // push(x) adds at the back, shift() takes from the front.
    const queue: [TreeNode, number][] = [];
    queue.push([root, 1]);
    while (queue.length > 0) {
        const pair = queue.shift()!;
        const node = pair[0];
        const depth = pair[1];
        // A leaf has no children. The first leaf we pop is the shallowest one.
        if (node.left === null && node.right === null) {
            return depth;
        }
        if (node.left !== null) {
            queue.push([node.left, depth + 1]);
        }
        if (node.right !== null) {
            queue.push([node.right, depth + 1]);
        }
    }
    return 0;  // never reached for a non-empty tree
}
class Solution {
    public int minDepth(TreeNode root) {
        if (root == null) {
            return 0;
        }
        // The queue holds (node, depth of that node). The root has depth 1.
        // offer(x) adds at the back, poll() takes from the front.
        Deque<Object[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.offer(new Object[] {root, 1});
        while (queue.size() > 0) {
            Object[] pair = queue.poll();
            TreeNode node = (TreeNode) pair[0];
            int depth = (Integer) pair[1];
            // A leaf has no children. The first leaf we pop is the shallowest one.
            if (node.left == null && node.right == null) {
                return depth;
            }
            if (node.left != null) {
                queue.offer(new Object[] {node.left, depth + 1});
            }
            if (node.right != null) {
                queue.offer(new Object[] {node.right, depth + 1});
            }
        }
        return 0;  // never reached for a non-empty tree
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. An empty tree has depth 0.
  2. The queue holds (node, depth) pairs, starting with (root, 1).
  3. Each pop is split into node = pair[0] and depth = pair[1].
  4. If the node has no left and no right child, it is a leaf. BFS pops nodes in depth order, so the first leaf we meet is the shallowest: return its depth right away.
  5. Otherwise queue each child that exists, one level deeper.

Dry run on root = [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] (answer 2):

Pop (node, depth)Leaf?Queue after
(3, 1)no, children 9 and 20[(9, 2), (20, 2)]
(9, 2)yes → return 2[(20, 2)] (never looked at)

Nodes 15 and 7 are never visited. That's the advantage over a DFS that would explore the whole tree.

Edge cases to test:

  • An empty tree → 0.
  • A chain of single children, e.g. [2, null, 3, null, 4] → 3 (not 1).
  • A single node → 1.

Complexity: O(n) worst case, but it stops at the first leaf. O(w) space.

Medium 1091. Shortest Path in Binary Matrix Google Meta Amazon Microsoft MatrixQueue

Problem: In an n × n grid of 0s (open) and 1s (blocked), find the length (number of cells) of the shortest path from the top-left to the bottom-right, moving in any of the 8 directions. Return -1 if there's no path.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: grid = [[0,1],[1,0]]
Output: 2
Example 2
Input: grid = [[0,0,0],[1,1,0],[1,1,0]]
Output: 4

Constraints: n == grid.length · n == grid[i].length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 100 · grid[i][j] is 0 or 1

Hint 1

Every move costs 1, and you may move in 8 directions.

Hint 2

BFS from (0, 0) through cells containing 0, counting path length; check the start and end cells first.

From brute force to the pattern: DFS tries many paths and doesn't naturally give the shortest. BFS reaches each cell first along a shortest path: O(n²).

Spot it: "shortest clear path" where every move costs 1, so grid BFS.

Approach:

  1. If the start or end cell is blocked, return -1.
  2. Enqueue (0, 0, 1), since the path length counts cells, and mark the start (set it to 1).
  3. Pop a cell. If it's the bottom-right, return its distance.
  4. For all 8 neighbours that are in bounds and open: mark them, then enqueue them with distance + 1.
class Solution:
    def shortestPathBinaryMatrix(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        size = len(grid)
        last = size - 1
        # A blocked start or a blocked end means there is no path at all.
        if grid[0][0] == 1 or grid[last][last] == 1:
            return -1
        # The queue holds (row, col, cells on the path so far). The start counts as 1.
        # append(x) adds at the back, popleft() takes from the front.
        queue = deque()
        queue.append((0, 0, 1))
        grid[0][0] = 1              # reuse the grid as "visited": 1 = blocked or visited
        while len(queue) > 0:
            item = queue.popleft()
            row = item[0]
            col = item[1]
            length = item[2]
            if row == last and col == last:
                return length
            # All 8 directions: the row and the col each change by -1, 0 or +1.
            for row_change in [-1, 0, 1]:
                for col_change in [-1, 0, 1]:
                    new_row = row + row_change
                    new_col = col + col_change
                    # Skip cells outside the grid.
                    if new_row < 0 or new_row >= size or new_col < 0 or new_col >= size:
                        continue
                    if grid[new_row][new_col] == 0:
                        grid[new_row][new_col] = 1      # mark on enqueue
                        queue.append((new_row, new_col, length + 1))
        return -1
function shortestPathBinaryMatrix(grid: number[][]): number {
    const size = grid.length;
    const last = size - 1;
    // A blocked start or a blocked end means there is no path at all.
    if (grid[0][0] === 1 || grid[last][last] === 1) {
        return -1;
    }
    // The queue holds [row, col, cells on the path so far]. The start counts as 1.
    // push(x) adds at the back; head moves forward instead of shift(), which is O(n).
    const queue: [number, number, number][] = [];
    queue.push([0, 0, 1]);
    grid[0][0] = 1;  // reuse the grid as "visited": 1 = blocked or visited
    let head = 0;
    while (head < queue.length) {
        const item = queue[head++];
        const row = item[0];
        const col = item[1];
        const length = item[2];
        if (row === last && col === last) {
            return length;
        }
        // All 8 directions: the row and the col each change by -1, 0 or +1.
        for (const rowChange of [-1, 0, 1]) {
            for (const colChange of [-1, 0, 1]) {
                const newRow = row + rowChange;
                const newCol = col + colChange;
                // Skip cells outside the grid.
                if (newRow < 0 || newRow >= size || newCol < 0 || newCol >= size) {
                    continue;
                }
                if (grid[newRow][newCol] === 0) {
                    grid[newRow][newCol] = 1;  // mark on enqueue
                    queue.push([newRow, newCol, length + 1]);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int shortestPathBinaryMatrix(int[][] grid) {
        int size = grid.length;
        int last = size - 1;
        // A blocked start or a blocked end means there is no path at all.
        if (grid[0][0] == 1 || grid[last][last] == 1) {
            return -1;
        }
        // The queue holds (row, col, cells on the path so far). The start counts as 1.
        // offer(x) adds at the back, poll() takes from the front.
        Deque<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.offer(new int[] {0, 0, 1});
        grid[0][0] = 1;  // reuse the grid as "visited": 1 = blocked or visited
        while (queue.size() > 0) {
            int[] item = queue.poll();
            int row = item[0];
            int col = item[1];
            int length = item[2];
            if (row == last && col == last) {
                return length;
            }
            // All 8 directions: the row and the col each change by -1, 0 or +1.
            for (int rowChange = -1; rowChange <= 1; rowChange++) {
                for (int colChange = -1; colChange <= 1; colChange++) {
                    int newRow = row + rowChange;
                    int newCol = col + colChange;
                    // Skip cells outside the grid.
                    if (newRow < 0 || newRow >= size || newCol < 0 || newCol >= size) {
                        continue;
                    }
                    if (grid[newRow][newCol] == 0) {
                        grid[newRow][newCol] = 1;  // mark on enqueue
                        queue.offer(new int[] {newRow, newCol, length + 1});
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. size is the grid width, last = size - 1 the index of the last row/column.
  2. If the start or the end cell is blocked, return -1 immediately.
  3. The queue holds (row, col, length), where length counts cells on the path, so the start is 1. Setting grid[0][0] = 1 marks it as visited (we reuse the grid instead of a separate set).
  4. Each pop is split into row, col, length by indexing. Popping the bottom-right cell means we're done.
  5. The two nested loops over [-1, 0, 1] try all 8 neighbours (the "no move" case lands on the current cell, which is already marked, so it's skipped).
  6. Cells outside the grid are skipped. An open cell (0) is marked 1 and queued with length + 1.

Edge cases to test:

  • The start or end cell is 1 → −1.
  • A 1 × 1 grid with a 0 → 1.
  • Diagonal shortcuts.
