                groups[x] = []  # these indices are queued now; never scan them again
            for j in targets:
                if 0 <= j < n and dist[j] == -1:
                    dist[j] = dist[i] + 1
                    queue.append(j)
        return -1
function minJumps(nums: number[]): number {
    const n = nums.length;
    const top = Math.max(...nums);
    const spf = Array.from({ length: top + 1 }, (_, i) => i);  // smallest prime factor of each number
    for (let p = 2; p * p <= top; p++) {
        if (spf[p] === p) {
            for (let m = p * p; m <= top; m += p) {
                if (spf[m] === m) {
                    spf[m] = p;
                }
            }
        }
    }
    const groups = new Map<number, number[]>();  // prime -> indices whose value it divides
    nums.forEach((value, j) => {
        let x = value;
        while (x > 1) {
            const p = spf[x];
            if (!groups.has(p)) {
                groups.set(p, []);
            }
            groups.get(p)!.push(j);
            while (x % p === 0) {
                x = x / p;
            }
        }
    });
    const dist: number[] = new Array(n).fill(-1);
    dist[0] = 0;
    const queue: number[] = [0];
    let head = 0;  // queue[head] is the front; shift() would be O(n)
    while (head < queue.length) {
        const i = queue[head++];
        if (i === n - 1) {
            return dist[i];
        }
        let targets = [i - 1, i + 1];
        const x = nums[i];
        if (x > 1 && spf[x] === x) {  // nums[i] is prime: teleport
            targets = targets.concat(groups.get(x) ?? []);
            groups.set(x, []);  // these indices are queued now; never scan them again
        }
        for (const j of targets) {
            if (0 <= j && j < n && dist[j] === -1) {
                dist[j] = dist[i] + 1;
                queue.push(j);
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int minJumps(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int top = 0;
        for (int x : nums) {
            top = Math.max(top, x);
        }
        int[] spf = new int[top + 1];  // smallest prime factor of each number
        for (int i = 0; i <= top; i++) {
            spf[i] = i;
        }
        for (int p = 2; (long) p * p <= top; p++) {
            if (spf[p] == p) {
                for (int m = p * p; m <= top; m += p) {
                    if (spf[m] == m) {
                        spf[m] = p;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        Map<Integer, List<Integer>> groups = new HashMap<>();  // prime -> indices whose value it divides
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            int x = nums[j];
            while (x > 1) {
                int p = spf[x];
                groups.computeIfAbsent(p, key -> new ArrayList<>()).add(j);
                while (x % p == 0) {
                    x /= p;
                }
            }
        }
        int[] dist = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(dist, -1);
        dist[0] = 0;
        Deque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(0));
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            int i = queue.poll();
            if (i == n - 1) {
                return dist[i];
            }
            List<Integer> targets = new ArrayList<>(List.of(i - 1, i + 1));
            int x = nums[i];
            if (x > 1 && spf[x] == x) {  // nums[i] is prime: teleport
                targets.addAll(groups.getOrDefault(x, List.of()));
                groups.put(x, new ArrayList<>());  // these indices are queued now; never scan them again
            }
            for (int j : targets) {
                if (0 <= j && j < n && dist[j] == -1) {
                    dist[j] = dist[i] + 1;
                    queue.offer(j);
                }
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The sieve gives each number's smallest prime factor, which lets us factor every value quickly.
  2. groups[p] lists exactly the indices a prime p can teleport to.
  3. After one teleport from any index with value p, all those targets are queued, so the group is emptied.
  4. BFS distances are the minimum jump counts.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • n = 1 → 0.
  • Value 1 (not prime, divisible by nothing).
  • Many copies of the same prime.

Complexity: O(M log log M + n log M) time for the sieve and factoring (M = max(nums)), O(M + n log M) space.

Hard 126. Word Ladder II Google Amazon Microsoft StringGraphQueueHash Map

Problem: Return all shortest transformation sequences from beginWord to endWord, changing one letter at a time through words of wordList.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: beginWord = "hit", endWord = "cog", wordList = ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log","cog"]
Output: [["hit","hot","dot","dog","cog"],["hit","hot","lot","log","cog"]]
Explanation: There are 2 shortest transformation sequences: "hit" -> "hot" -> "dot" -> "dog" -> "cog" "hit" -> "hot" -> "lot" -> "log" -> "cog"
Example 2
Input: beginWord = "hit", endWord = "cog", wordList = ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log"]
Output: []
Explanation: The endWord "cog" is not in wordList, therefore there is no valid transformation sequence.

Constraints: 1 ≤ beginWord.length ≤ 5 · endWord.length == beginWord.length · 1 ≤ wordList.length ≤ 500 · wordList[i].length == beginWord.length · beginWord, endWord, and wordList[i] consist of lowercase English letters. · beginWord != endWord · All the words in wordList are unique. · The sum of all shortest transformation sequences does not exceed 10⁵.

Hint 1

Find the shortest distance first with BFS.

Hint 2

While doing BFS, remember all parents of each word that lie on a shortest path.

Hint 3

Rebuild every ladder by backtracking from the end word.

From brute force to the pattern: DFS over every transformation sequence is exponential. BFS with parent sets keeps only shortest-path edges.

Spot it: Shortest → BFS. All shortest paths → during BFS, record for each word every word on the previous layer that leads to it (its parents), and only expand words not seen in earlier layers. Then backtrack from endWord through the parents.

Why not another pattern? DFS over all paths explores exponentially many long paths; storing full paths in the BFS queue blows up memory.

Approach:

  1. BFS from beginWord one layer at a time; remove the whole layer from the word set before expanding it.
  2. For each word, try all one-letter changes; any that is in the set gets this word added to its parents.
  3. Stop after the layer that reaches endWord.
  4. Backtrack from endWord to beginWord through parents, building each path in reverse.
from collections import defaultdict

class Solution:
    def findLadders(self, beginWord: str, endWord: str, wordList: List[str]) -> List[List[str]]:
        words = set(wordList)
        if endWord not in words:
            return []
        parents = defaultdict(set)  # word -> words one layer earlier that lead to it
        layer = {beginWord}
        words.discard(beginWord)
        found = False
        while layer and not found:
            nxt = defaultdict(set)
            for word in layer:
                for i in range(len(word)):
                    for ch in "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz":
                        cand = word[:i] + ch + word[i + 1:]
                        if cand in words:
                            nxt[cand].add(word)  # one more shortest way into cand
                            if cand == endWord:
                                found = True
            words -= nxt.keys()  # words reached now can't appear on a later layer
            for w, ps in nxt.items():
                parents[w] |= ps
            layer = set(nxt)
        if not found:
            return []
        ladders = []
        path = [endWord]

        def back(word):
            if word == beginWord:
                ladders.append(path[::-1])  # reached the start: one full ladder
                return
            for p in parents[word]:
                path.append(p)
                back(p)
                path.pop()

        back(endWord)
        return ladders
function findLadders(beginWord: string, endWord: string, wordList: string[]): string[][] {
    const words = new Set(wordList);
    if (!words.has(endWord)) {
        return [];
    }
    const parents = new Map<string, Set<string>>();  // word -> words one layer earlier that lead to it
    let layer = new Set<string>([beginWord]);
    words.delete(beginWord);
    let found = false;
    while (layer.size > 0 && !found) {
        const nxt = new Map<string, Set<string>>();
        for (const word of layer) {
            for (let i = 0; i < word.length; i++) {
                for (const ch of "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz") {
                    const cand = word.slice(0, i) + ch + word.slice(i + 1);
                    if (words.has(cand)) {
                        if (!nxt.has(cand)) {
                            nxt.set(cand, new Set());
                        }
                        nxt.get(cand)!.add(word);  // one more shortest way into cand
                        if (cand === endWord) {
                            found = true;
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        for (const w of nxt.keys()) {
            words.delete(w);  // words reached now can't appear on a later layer
        }
        for (const [w, ps] of nxt) {
            if (!parents.has(w)) {
                parents.set(w, new Set());
            }
            for (const p of ps) {
                parents.get(w)!.add(p);
            }
        }
        layer = new Set(nxt.keys());
    }
    if (!found) {
        return [];
    }
    const ladders: string[][] = [];
    const path: string[] = [endWord];

    const back = (word: string): void => {
        if (word === beginWord) {
            ladders.push([...path].reverse());  // reached the start: one full ladder
            return;
        }
        for (const p of parents.get(word) ?? []) {
            path.push(p);
            back(p);
            path.pop();
        }
    };

    back(endWord);
    return ladders;
}
class Solution {
    private Map<String, Set<String>> parents;
    private List<List<String>> ladders;
    private List<String> path;
    private String beginWord;

    public List<List<String>> findLadders(String beginWord, String endWord, List<String> wordList) {
        Set<String> words = new HashSet<>(wordList);
        if (!words.contains(endWord)) {
            return new ArrayList<>();
        }
        parents = new HashMap<>();  // word -> words one layer earlier that lead to it
        Set<String> layer = new HashSet<>(Set.of(beginWord));
        words.remove(beginWord);
        boolean found = false;
        while (!layer.isEmpty() && !found) {
            Map<String, Set<String>> nxt = new HashMap<>();
            for (String word : layer) {
                char[] chars = word.toCharArray();
                for (int i = 0; i < chars.length; i++) {
                    char orig = chars[i];
                    for (char ch = 'a'; ch <= 'z'; ch++) {
                        chars[i] = ch;
                        String cand = new String(chars);
                        if (words.contains(cand)) {
                            nxt.computeIfAbsent(cand, key -> new HashSet<>()).add(word);  // one more shortest way into cand
                            if (cand.equals(endWord)) {
                                found = true;
                            }
                        }
                    }
                    chars[i] = orig;
                }
            }
            words.removeAll(nxt.keySet());  // words reached now can't appear on a later layer
            for (Map.Entry<String, Set<String>> e : nxt.entrySet()) {
                parents.computeIfAbsent(e.getKey(), key -> new HashSet<>()).addAll(e.getValue());
            }
            layer = new HashSet<>(nxt.keySet());
        }
        ladders = new ArrayList<>();
        if (!found) {
            return ladders;
        }
        this.beginWord = beginWord;
        path = new ArrayList<>(List.of(endWord));
        back(endWord);
        return ladders;
    }

    private void back(String word) {
        if (word.equals(beginWord)) {
            List<String> ladder = new ArrayList<>(path);
            Collections.reverse(ladder);
            ladders.add(ladder);  // reached the start: one full ladder
            return;
        }
        for (String p : parents.getOrDefault(word, Set.of())) {
            path.add(p);
            back(p);
            path.remove(path.size() - 1);
        }
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Words are removed from the set only after a whole layer is processed, so several words of the same layer can all become parents of one word.
  2. A word reached in an earlier layer is never used again, which keeps every recorded edge on a shortest path.
  3. Backtracking from endWord follows only shortest-path edges, so every path found has minimum length.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • endWord not in the list → [].
  • Several shortest ladders sharing words.
  • beginWord one step from endWord.

Complexity: O(N · L · 26) for the BFS (N words of length L) plus the size of the output for backtracking.

Hard 864. Shortest Path to Get All Keys Google MatrixQueueHash Set

Problem: In a grid with walls, keys a–f and locks A–F, return the fewest moves from @ to collect every key, or −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: grid = ["@.a..","###.#","b.A.B"]
Output: 8
Explanation: Note that the goal is to obtain all the keys not to open all the locks.
Example 2
Input: grid = ["@..aA","..B#.","....b"]
Output: 6

Constraints: m == grid.length · n == grid[i].length · 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 30 · grid[i][j] is either an English letter, '.', '#', or '@'. · There is exactly one '@' in the grid. · The number of keys in the grid is in the range [1, 6]. · Each key in the grid is unique. · Each key in the grid has a matching lock.

Hint 1

BFS on cells is not enough. What else describes where you are in the search?

Hint 2

Add the set of collected keys (as a bitmask) to the BFS state.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying every key order (K!) with a BFS for each leg is slower and trickier; BFS over (cell, mask) handles it in one search.

Spot it: Shortest moves on a grid → BFS, but the position alone isn't the state: what you can do depends on the keys held. Use state (r, c, mask) where mask has a bit per key (at most 2⁶ = 64 masks).

Why not another pattern? BFS on cells alone forbids revisiting a cell after picking up a key, which is often necessary.

Approach:

  1. Find @ and the number of keys; goal = (1 << keys) − 1.
  2. BFS from (start, mask 0). Skip walls and locks whose key bit isn't set.
  3. Stepping on a key sets its bit. Return the distance when mask == goal.
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def shortestPathAllKeys(self, grid: List[str]) -> int:
        rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        keys = 0
        for r in range(rows):
            for c in range(cols):
                if grid[r][c] == "@":
                    start = (r, c)
                elif grid[r][c].islower():
                    keys += 1
        goal = (1 << keys) - 1  # every key bit set
        queue = deque([(start[0], start[1], 0, 0)])  # row, col, keys held, moves
        seen = {(start[0], start[1], 0)}
        while queue:
            r, c, mask, moves = queue.popleft()
            for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                if not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols) or grid[nr][nc] == "#":
                    continue
                cell = grid[nr][nc]
                if cell.isupper() and not mask >> (ord(cell) - ord("A")) & 1:
                    continue  # locked and we don't have the key
                nmask = mask
                if cell.islower():
                    nmask = mask | 1 << (ord(cell) - ord("a"))  # pick up the key
                if nmask == goal:
                    return moves + 1
                if (nr, nc, nmask) not in seen:
                    seen.add((nr, nc, nmask))
                    queue.append((nr, nc, nmask, moves + 1))
        return -1
function shortestPathAllKeys(grid: string[]): number {
    const rows = grid.length, cols = grid[0].length;
    let keys = 0;
    let start: [number, number] = [0, 0];
    for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++) {
        for (let c = 0; c < cols; c++) {
            if (grid[r][c] === "@") {
                start = [r, c];
            } else if (grid[r][c] >= "a" && grid[r][c] <= "z") {
                keys += 1;
            }
        }
    }
    const goal = (1 << keys) - 1;  // every key bit set
    const queue: [number, number, number, number][] = [[start[0], start[1], 0, 0]];  // row, col, keys held, moves
    const seen = new Set<string>([`${start[0]},${start[1]},0`]);
    let head = 0;  // queue[head] is the front; shift() would be O(n)
    while (head < queue.length) {
        const [r, c, mask, moves] = queue[head++];
        for (const [nr, nc] of [[r + 1, c], [r - 1, c], [r, c + 1], [r, c - 1]]) {
            if (!(0 <= nr && nr < rows && 0 <= nc && nc < cols) || grid[nr][nc] === "#") {
                continue;
            }
            const cell = grid[nr][nc];
            if (cell >= "A" && cell <= "Z" && !((mask >> (cell.charCodeAt(0) - 65)) & 1)) {
                continue;  // locked and we don't have the key
            }
            let nmask = mask;
            if (cell >= "a" && cell <= "z") {
                nmask = mask | (1 << (cell.charCodeAt(0) - 97));  // pick up the key
            }
            if (nmask === goal) {
                return moves + 1;
            }
            const state = `${nr},${nc},${nmask}`;
            if (!seen.has(state)) {
                seen.add(state);
                queue.push([nr, nc, nmask, moves + 1]);
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int shortestPathAllKeys(String[] grid) {
        int rows = grid.length, cols = grid[0].length();
        int keys = 0;
        int[] start = {0, 0};
        for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++) {
                char ch = grid[r].charAt(c);
                if (ch == '@') {
                    start = new int[] {r, c};
                } else if (Character.isLowerCase(ch)) {
                    keys += 1;
                }
            }
        }
        int goal = (1 << keys) - 1;  // every key bit set
        Deque<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();  // row, col, keys held, moves
        queue.offer(new int[] {start[0], start[1], 0, 0});
        boolean[][][] seen = new boolean[rows][cols][goal + 1];
        seen[start[0]][start[1]][0] = true;
        int[][] dirs = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            int[] item = queue.poll();
            int r = item[0], c = item[1], mask = item[2], moves = item[3];
            for (int[] d : dirs) {
                int nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1];
                if (!(0 <= nr && nr < rows && 0 <= nc && nc < cols) || grid[nr].charAt(nc) == '#') {
                    continue;
                }
                char cell = grid[nr].charAt(nc);
                if (Character.isUpperCase(cell) && (mask >> (cell - 'A') & 1) == 0) {
                    continue;  // locked and we don't have the key
                }
                int nmask = mask;
                if (Character.isLowerCase(cell)) {
                    nmask = mask | 1 << (cell - 'a');  // pick up the key
                }
                if (nmask == goal) {
                    return moves + 1;
                }
                if (!seen[nr][nc][nmask]) {
                    seen[nr][nc][nmask] = true;
                    queue.offer(new int[] {nr, nc, nmask, moves + 1});
                }
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The state includes the keys held, so revisiting a cell with more keys is allowed and useful.
  2. A lock is passable only when its key's bit is set in the mask.
  3. BFS reaches every state in the fewest moves, so the first time the mask is complete is optimal.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • A lock blocks the only path to its own key → −1.
  • Keys collected in a non-obvious order.
  • A single key next to the start.

Complexity: O(m · n · 2ᴷ) time and space (K ≤ 6 keys).

Hard 1345. Jump Game IV Google Amazon ArrayHash MapQueue

Problem: From index i you can move to i − 1, i + 1, or any j with arr[j] == arr[i]. Return the fewest steps from index 0 to the last index.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: arr = [100,-23,-23,404,100,23,23,23,3,404]
Output: 3
Explanation: You need three jumps from index 0 --> 4 --> 3 --> 9. Note that index 9 is the last index of the array.
Example 2
Input: arr = [7]
Output: 0
Explanation: Start index is the last index. You do not need to jump.

Constraints: 1 ≤ arr.length ≤ 5 * 10⁴ · -10⁸ ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10⁸

Hint 1

This is a shortest path in an unweighted graph: BFS.

Hint 2

Equal values create many edges. After you've used a value's teleport once, do you ever need it again?

From brute force to the pattern: Scanning each value group from every index is O(n²) for repeated values. Clearing groups after first use makes BFS O(n).

Spot it: Fewest steps on an unweighted graph → BFS. The catch: equal values form cliques with up to n² edges. Once a value's group has been expanded, every member is already queued, so delete the group to never scan it again.

Why not another pattern? Plain BFS rescanning each value group from every member is O(n²) on arrays like [7,7,7,…].

Approach:

  1. Map each value to its list of indices.
  2. BFS from 0; neighbours: i − 1, i + 1, and every index in groups[arr[i]].
  3. After using groups[arr[i]], clear it.
  4. Return the layer when the last index is reached.
from collections import defaultdict, deque

class Solution:
    def minJumps(self, arr: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(arr)
        groups = defaultdict(list)
        for i, x in enumerate(arr):
            groups[x].append(i)
        seen = [False] * n
        seen[0] = True
        queue = deque([0])
        steps = 0
        while queue:
            for _ in range(len(queue)):
                i = queue.popleft()
                if i == n - 1:
                    return steps
                for j in groups[arr[i]] + [i - 1, i + 1]:
                    if 0 <= j < n and not seen[j]:
                        seen[j] = True
                        queue.append(j)
                groups[arr[i]] = []  # every equal-valued index is queued now: never scan them again
            steps += 1
        return -1
function minJumps(arr: number[]): number {
    const n = arr.length;
    const groups = new Map<number, number[]>();
    arr.forEach((x, i) => {
        if (!groups.has(x)) {
            groups.set(x, []);
        }
        groups.get(x)!.push(i);
    });
    const seen: boolean[] = new Array(n).fill(false);
    seen[0] = true;
    let queue: number[] = [0];
    let steps = 0;
    while (queue.length > 0) {
        const next: number[] = [];
        for (const i of queue) {
            if (i === n - 1) {
                return steps;
            }
            for (const j of [...groups.get(arr[i])!, i - 1, i + 1]) {
                if (0 <= j && j < n && !seen[j]) {
                    seen[j] = true;
                    next.push(j);
                }
            }
            groups.set(arr[i], []);  // every equal-valued index is queued now: never scan them again
        }
        queue = next;
        steps += 1;
    }
    return -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int minJumps(int[] arr) {
        int n = arr.length;
        Map<Integer, List<Integer>> groups = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            groups.computeIfAbsent(arr[i], key -> new ArrayList<>()).add(i);
        }
        boolean[] seen = new boolean[n];
        seen[0] = true;
        Deque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(0));
        int steps = 0;
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            for (int k = queue.size(); k > 0; k--) {
                int i = queue.poll();
                if (i == n - 1) {
                    return steps;
                }
                List<Integer> jumps = new ArrayList<>(groups.get(arr[i]));
                jumps.add(i - 1);
                jumps.add(i + 1);
                for (int j : jumps) {
                    if (0 <= j && j < n && !seen[j]) {
                        seen[j] = true;
                        queue.offer(j);
                    }
                }
                groups.put(arr[i], new ArrayList<>());  // every equal-valued index is queued now: never scan them again
            }
            steps += 1;
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The value groups are the teleport edges.
  2. Clearing a group after one use is what keeps the BFS linear: each group is scanned once in total.
  3. BFS layers count steps, so reaching n − 1 returns the minimum.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • n = 1 → 0.
  • All values equal → 1 step.
  • No repeated values (only ±1 moves).

Complexity: O(n) time and space.

Hard 2045. Second Minimum Time to Reach Destination Google GraphQueue

Problem: Every edge takes time minutes; all signals toggle green/red every change minutes and you may leave only on green. Return the second smallest (strictly larger) arrival time from 1 to n.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 5, edges = [[1,2],[1,3],[1,4],[3,4],[4,5]], time = 3, change = 5
Output: 13
Explanation: The figure on the left shows the given graph. The blue path in the figure on the right is the minimum time path. The time taken is: - Start at 1, time elapsed=0 - 1 -> 4: 3 minutes, time elapsed=3 - 4 -> 5: 3 minutes, time elapsed=6 Hence the minimum time needed is 6 minutes. The red path shows the path to get the second minimum time. - Start at 1, time elapsed=0 - 1 -> 3: 3 minutes, time elapsed=3 - 3 -> 4: 3 minutes, time elapsed=6 - Wait at 4 for 4 minutes, time elapsed=10 - 4 -> 5: 3 minutes, time elapsed=13 Hence the second minimum time is 13 minutes.
Example 2
Input: n = 2, edges = [[1,2]], time = 3, change = 2
Output: 11
Explanation: The minimum time path is 1 -> 2 with time = 3 minutes. The second minimum time path is 1 -> 2 -> 1 -> 2 with time = 11 minutes.

Constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴ · n - 1 ≤ edges.length ≤ min(2 * 10⁴, n * (n - 1) / 2) · edges[i].length == 2 · 1 ≤ ui, vi ≤ n · ui != vi · There are no duplicate edges. · Each vertex can be reached directly or indirectly from every other vertex. · 1 ≤ time, change ≤ 10³

Hint 1

Does the arrival time depend on anything except the number of edges walked?

Hint 2

Find the second smallest number of edges from 1 to n: BFS that allows two visits per node.

Hint 3

Then simulate the traffic lights along that many edges.

From brute force to the pattern: Enumerating paths is exponential; Dijkstra over (node, rank) works but a two-visit BFS is simpler and linear.

Spot it: Signals are shared, so total time depends only on the number of edges walked: fewer edges is always faster. So find the second smallest distinct path length (in edges) with a BFS that lets each node be reached twice (first and second distinct distance), then simulate the signals along that many edges.

Why not another pattern? Dijkstra on times works but is overkill; time is monotone in edge count, so BFS on counts is enough.

Approach:

  1. BFS storing first[v] and second[v] (distinct edge counts).
  2. When reaching v with distance d: if first is unset, set it; elif d > first[v] and second is unset, set second. Enqueue only on such updates.
  3. Simulate second[n] edges: before each edge, if the light is red ((t // change) % 2 == 1), wait until it turns green; then add time.
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def secondMinimum(self, n: int, edges: List[List[int]], time: int, change: int) -> int:
        adj = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
        for a, b in edges:
            adj[a].append(b)
            adj[b].append(a)
        first = [-1] * (n + 1)  # shortest edge count to each node
        second = [-1] * (n + 1)  # second shortest (strictly larger)
        first[1] = 0
        queue = deque([(1, 0)])
        while queue:
            u, d = queue.popleft()
            for v in adj[u]:
                if first[v] == -1:
                    first[v] = d + 1
                    queue.append((v, d + 1))
                elif second[v] == -1 and d + 1 > first[v]:
                    second[v] = d + 1  # a strictly longer way in
                    queue.append((v, d + 1))
        t = 0
        for _ in range(second[n]):  # walk that many edges
            if (t // change) % 2 == 1:
                t = (t // change + 1) * change  # red: wait for green
            t += time
        return t
function secondMinimum(n: number, edges: number[][], time: number, change: number): number {
    const adj: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n + 1 }, () => []);
    for (const [a, b] of edges) {
        adj[a].push(b);
        adj[b].push(a);
    }
    const first: number[] = new Array(n + 1).fill(-1);   // shortest edge count to each node
    const second: number[] = new Array(n + 1).fill(-1);  // second shortest (strictly larger)
    first[1] = 0;
    const queue: [number, number][] = [[1, 0]];
    let head = 0;  // queue[head] is the front; shift() would be O(n)
    while (head < queue.length) {
        const [u, d] = queue[head++];
        for (const v of adj[u]) {
            if (first[v] === -1) {
                first[v] = d + 1;
                queue.push([v, d + 1]);
            } else if (second[v] === -1 && d + 1 > first[v]) {
                second[v] = d + 1;  // a strictly longer way in
                queue.push([v, d + 1]);
            }
        }
    }
    let t = 0;
    for (let k = 0; k < second[n]; k++) {  // walk that many edges
        if (Math.floor(t / change) % 2 === 1) {
            t = (Math.floor(t / change) + 1) * change;  // red: wait for green
        }
        t += time;
    }
    return t;
}
class Solution {
    public int secondMinimum(int n, int[][] edges, int time, int change) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
            adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
        }
        for (int[] e : edges) {
            adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]);
            adj.get(e[1]).add(e[0]);
        }
        int[] first = new int[n + 1];   // shortest edge count to each node
        int[] second = new int[n + 1];  // second shortest (strictly larger)
        Arrays.fill(first, -1);
        Arrays.fill(second, -1);
        first[1] = 0;
        Deque<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.offer(new int[] {1, 0});
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            int[] item = queue.poll();
            int u = item[0], d = item[1];
            for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
                if (first[v] == -1) {
                    first[v] = d + 1;
                    queue.offer(new int[] {v, d + 1});
                } else if (second[v] == -1 && d + 1 > first[v]) {
                    second[v] = d + 1;  // a strictly longer way in
                    queue.offer(new int[] {v, d + 1});
                }
            }
        }
        int t = 0;
        for (int k = 0; k < second[n]; k++) {  // walk that many edges
            if ((t / change) % 2 == 1) {
                t = (t / change + 1) * change;  // red: wait for green
            }
            t += time;
        }
        return t;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Everyone sees the same signal schedule, so a path with more edges never arrives earlier: comparing edge counts is enough.
  2. Each node is enqueued at most twice (first and second distance), keeping the BFS linear.
  3. The second distinct count always exists: you can bounce back and forth on an edge to add 2.
  4. The simulation waits whenever the light is red at departure, then traverses the edge.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Second path is the shortest + 2 (bouncing on an edge).
  • Waiting at red lights.
  • n = 2 with a single edge.

Complexity: O(n + e) time and space.

Medium 1162. As Far from Land as Possible Amazon MatrixQueue

Problem: Find a water cell whose distance to the nearest land is maximal (Manhattan), or −1 if there's no land or no water.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: grid = [[1,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,1]]
Output: 2
Explanation: The cell (1, 1) is as far as possible from all the land with distance 2.
Example 2
Input: grid = [[1,0,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,0]]
Output: 4
Explanation: The cell (2, 2) is as far as possible from all the land with distance 4.

Constraints: n == grid.length · n == grid[i].length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 100 · grid[i][j] is 0 or 1

Hint 1

Compute the distance to the nearest land for every cell.

Hint 2

Start BFS from all land cells at once.

From brute force to the pattern: BFS per water cell is O(n⁴); multi-source BFS is O(n²).

Spot it: Distance to the nearest land for every cell → multi-source BFS starting from all land at once; BFS layers are the distances.

Why not another pattern? BFS from each water cell separately is O(n⁴).

Approach:

  1. Queue all land cells.
  2. BFS layer by layer into water, marking visited.
  3. The number of layers processed is the answer (−1 if no water or no land).
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def maxDistance(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(grid)
        queue = deque((r, c) for r in range(n) for c in range(n) if grid[r][c] == 1)
        if len(queue) in (0, n * n):
            return -1  # no land, or no water
        dist = -1
        while queue:
            dist += 1
            for _ in range(len(queue)):
                r, c = queue.popleft()
                for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                    if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and grid[nr][nc] == 0:
                        grid[nr][nc] = 1  # reached: mark as visited
                        queue.append((nr, nc))
        return dist
function maxDistance(grid: number[][]): number {
    const n = grid.length;
    let queue: [number, number][] = [];
    for (let r = 0; r < n; r++) {
        for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            if (grid[r][c] === 1) {
                queue.push([r, c]);
            }
        }
    }
    if (queue.length === 0 || queue.length === n * n) {
        return -1;  // no land, or no water
    }
    let dist = -1;
    while (queue.length > 0) {
        dist += 1;
        const next: [number, number][] = [];
        for (const [r, c] of queue) {
            for (const [nr, nc] of [[r + 1, c], [r - 1, c], [r, c + 1], [r, c - 1]]) {
                if (0 <= nr && nr < n && 0 <= nc && nc < n && grid[nr][nc] === 0) {
                    grid[nr][nc] = 1;  // reached: mark as visited
                    next.push([nr, nc]);
                }
            }
        }
        queue = next;
    }
    return dist;
}
class Solution {
    public int maxDistance(int[][] grid) {
        int n = grid.length;
        Deque<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int r = 0; r < n; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                if (grid[r][c] == 1) {
                    queue.offer(new int[] {r, c});
                }
            }
        }
        if (queue.size() == 0 || queue.size() == n * n) {
            return -1;  // no land, or no water
        }
        int[][] dirs = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
        int dist = -1;
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            dist += 1;
            for (int k = queue.size(); k > 0; k--) {
                int[] cell = queue.poll();
                for (int[] d : dirs) {
                    int nr = cell[0] + d[0], nc = cell[1] + d[1];
                    if (0 <= nr && nr < n && 0 <= nc && nc < n && grid[nr][nc] == 0) {
                        grid[nr][nc] = 1;  // reached: mark as visited
                        queue.offer(new int[] {nr, nc});
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return dist;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. All land starts at distance 0, so a water cell is first reached at its distance to the nearest land.
  2. In a grid without obstacles, BFS steps equal Manhattan distance.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • All land or all water → −1.
  • One land cell.
  • Land in the middle.

Complexity: O(n²) time and space.

Medium 1236. Web Crawler Amazon Microsoft StringHash SetQueue

Problem: Using htmlParser.getUrls(url), crawl every page reachable from startUrl on the same hostname (any order).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ (Premium)

Example 1
Input: urls = ["http://news.yahoo.com","http://news.yahoo.com/news","http://news.yahoo.com/news/topics/","http://news.google.com","http://news.yahoo.com/us"], edges = [[2,0],[2,1],[3,2],[3,1],[0,4]], startUrl = "http://news.yahoo.com/news/topics/"
Output: ["http://news.yahoo.com","http://news.yahoo.com/news","http://news.yahoo.com/news/topics/","http://news.yahoo.com/us"]
Explanation: news.google.com is a different host, so it's skipped.
Example 2
Input: urls = ["http://news.yahoo.com","http://news.yahoo.com/news","http://news.yahoo.com/news/topics/","http://news.google.com"], edges = [[0,2],[2,1],[3,2],[3,1],[3,0]], startUrl = "http://news.google.com"
Output: ["http://news.google.com"]
Explanation: Every link from the start page goes to another host.

Constraints: 1 ≤ urls.length ≤ 1000 · 1 ≤ urls[i].length ≤ 300 · startUrl is one of the urls · Hostname label must be from 1 to 63 characters long, including the dots, may contain only the ASCII letters from 'a' to 'z', digits from '0' to '9' and the hyphen-minus character ('-') · You may assume there're no duplicates in the URL library

Hint 1

The pages and links form a graph.

Hint 2

Traverse it, staying on the same hostname.

From brute force to the pattern: This is the plain traversal; the visited set is what makes it finite.

Spot it: Pages and links are a graph; visit everything reachable → BFS (or DFS) with a visited set, filtered by hostname.

Why not another pattern? Recursion without a visited set loops forever on cyclic links.

Approach:

  1. host = startUrl.split('/')[2].
  2. BFS from startUrl; for each link with the same host and not seen, enqueue it.
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def crawl(self, startUrl: str, htmlParser: "HtmlParser") -> List[str]:
        host = startUrl.split("/")[2]  # "http://host/path" -> host
        seen = {startUrl}
        queue = deque([startUrl])
        while queue:
            url = queue.popleft()
            for link in htmlParser.getUrls(url):
                if link not in seen and link.split("/")[2] == host:
                    seen.add(link)  # same site, not visited yet
                    queue.append(link)
        return list(seen)
/**
 * // This is the HtmlParser's API interface.
 * // You should not implement it, or speculate about its implementation
 * interface HtmlParser {
 *     getUrls(url: string): string[] {}
 * }
 */
function crawl(startUrl: string, htmlParser: HtmlParser): string[] {
    const host = startUrl.split("/")[2];  // "http://host/path" -> host
    const seen = new Set<string>([startUrl]);
    const queue: string[] = [startUrl];
    while (queue.length > 0) {
        const url = queue.shift()!;
        for (const link of htmlParser.getUrls(url)) {
            if (!seen.has(link) && link.split("/")[2] === host) {
                seen.add(link);  // same site, not visited yet
                queue.push(link);
            }
        }
    }
    return [...seen];
}
/**
 * // This is the HtmlParser's API interface.
 * // You should not implement it, or speculate about its implementation
 * interface HtmlParser {
 *     public List<String> getUrls(String url) {}
 * }
 */
class Solution {
    public List<String> crawl(String startUrl, HtmlParser htmlParser) {
        String host = startUrl.split("/")[2];  // "http://host/path" -> host
        Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>(Set.of(startUrl));
        Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(startUrl));
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            String url = queue.poll();
            for (String link : htmlParser.getUrls(url)) {
                if (!seen.contains(link) && link.split("/")[2].equals(host)) {
                    seen.add(link);  // same site, not visited yet
                    queue.offer(link);
                }
            }
        }
        return new ArrayList<>(seen);
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Splitting on / gives ['http:', '', host, …].
  2. Marking URLs when enqueued avoids duplicates in the queue.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Links to other hosts (skip).
  • Cycles of links.
  • Pages with no links.

Complexity: O(V + E) time over pages and links, O(V) space.

Medium 1311. Get Watched Videos by Your Friends Amazon GraphQueueHash Map

Problem: Return the videos watched by people at shortest distance exactly level from id, ordered by frequency then name.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: watchedVideos = [["A","B"],["C"],["B","C"],["D"]], friends = [[1,2],[0,3],[0,3],[1,2]], id = 0, level = 1
Output: ["B","C"]
Explanation: You have id = 0 (green color in the figure) and your friends are (yellow color in the figure): Person with id = 1 -> watchedVideos = ["C"] Person with id = 2 -> watchedVideos = ["B","C"] The frequencies of watchedVideos by your friends are: B -> 1 C -> 2
Example 2
Input: watchedVideos = [["A","B"],["C"],["B","C"],["D"]], friends = [[1,2],[0,3],[0,3],[1,2]], id = 0, level = 2
Output: ["D"]
Explanation: You have id = 0 (green color in the figure) and the only friend of your friends is the person with id = 3 (yellow color in the figure).

Constraints: n == watchedVideos.length == friends.length · 2 ≤ n ≤ 100 · 1 ≤ watchedVideos[i].length ≤ 100 · 1 ≤ watchedVideos[i][j].length ≤ 8 · 0 ≤ friends[i].length < n · 0 ≤ friends[i][j] < n · 0 ≤ id < n · 1 ≤ level < n · if friends[i] contains j, then friends[j] contains i

Hint 1

Find the people at shortest distance exactly level.

Hint 2

Count their videos and sort.

From brute force to the pattern: DFS can reach people through longer paths; BFS layers are exact.

Spot it: "Friends at distance exactly k" → BFS by layers. Then count videos with a hash map and sort.

Why not another pattern? DFS doesn't give shortest distances.

Approach:

  1. BFS from id for level layers with a visited set.
  2. Count videos of the people in the final layer.
  3. Sort by (count, name).
from collections import Counter

class Solution:
    def watchedVideosByFriends(self, watchedVideos: List[List[str]], friends: List[List[int]], id: int, level: int) -> List[str]:
        seen = {id}
        layer = [id]
        for _ in range(level):  # move out one layer at a time
            nxt = []
            for p in layer:
                for f in friends[p]:
                    if f not in seen:
                        seen.add(f)
                        nxt.append(f)
            layer = nxt
        count = Counter(v for p in layer for v in watchedVideos[p])
        return sorted(count, key=lambda v: (count[v], v))  # rarest first, then alphabetical
function watchedVideosByFriends(watchedVideos: string[][], friends: number[][], id: number, level: number): string[] {
    const seen = new Set<number>([id]);
    let layer: number[] = [id];
    for (let k = 0; k < level; k++) {  // move out one layer at a time
        const nxt: number[] = [];
        for (const p of layer) {
            for (const f of friends[p]) {
                if (!seen.has(f)) {
                    seen.add(f);
                    nxt.push(f);
                }
            }
        }
        layer = nxt;
    }
    const count = new Map<string, number>();
    for (const p of layer) {
        for (const v of watchedVideos[p]) {
            count.set(v, (count.get(v) ?? 0) + 1);
        }
    }
    // rarest first, then alphabetical
    return [...count.keys()].sort((a, b) => count.get(a)! - count.get(b)! || (a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0));
}
class Solution {
    public List<String> watchedVideosByFriends(List<List<String>> watchedVideos, int[][] friends, int id, int level) {
        Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>(Set.of(id));
        List<Integer> layer = new ArrayList<>(List.of(id));
        for (int k = 0; k < level; k++) {  // move out one layer at a time
            List<Integer> nxt = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int p : layer) {
                for (int f : friends[p]) {
                    if (!seen.contains(f)) {
                        seen.add(f);
                        nxt.add(f);
                    }
                }
            }
            layer = nxt;
        }
        Map<String, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
        for (int p : layer) {
            for (String v : watchedVideos.get(p)) {
                count.merge(v, 1, Integer::sum);
            }
        }
        List<String> result = new ArrayList<>(count.keySet());
        // rarest first, then alphabetical
        result.sort((a, b) -> !count.get(a).equals(count.get(b)) ? Integer.compare(count.get(a), count.get(b)) : a.compareTo(b));
        return result;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Marking people as seen when first reached keeps only shortest distances.
  2. Sorting by (frequency, name) matches the required order.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Level beyond everyone → [].
  • Ties in frequency (alphabetical).
  • A person reachable at several distances.

Complexity: O(V + E + W log W) time, where W is the number of distinct videos.

Medium 3552. Grid Teleportation Traversal Amazon MatrixDequeHash Map

Problem: Move up/down/left/right (cost 1) avoiding #; stepping on a letter lets you teleport to any same letter for free, once per letter. Return the fewest moves.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: matrix = [".#...",".#.#.",".#.#.","...#."]
Output: 13

Constraints: 1 ≤ m == matrix.length ≤ 10³ · 1 ≤ n == matrix[i].length ≤ 10³ · matrix[i][j] is either '#', '.', or an uppercase English letter. · matrix[0][0] is not an obstacle.

Hint 1

Teleporting is free and moving costs 1: which BFS handles 0/1 weights?

Hint 2

Is it ever useful to teleport with the same letter twice?

From brute force to the pattern: Tracking used letters in the state is 2²⁶ times bigger; using each letter at its first (cheapest) visit is enough.

Spot it: Edges of weight 0 (teleport) and 1 (move) → 0-1 BFS with a deque. Like Jump Game IV, expand each letter's portal group only the first time that letter is popped (the earliest pop has the smallest distance, so later uses can't help).

Why not another pattern? Plain BFS mishandles zero-cost teleports; tracking which letters were used in the state blows up.

Approach:

  1. Group cells by letter.
  2. Deque from (0, 0) with distance 0.
  3. Pop a cell; if it's an unused letter, set every same-letter cell to this distance (push front).
  4. Normal moves cost 1 (push back).
from collections import defaultdict, deque

class Solution:
    def minMoves(self, matrix: List[str]) -> int:
        m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        portals = defaultdict(list)
        for r in range(m):
            for c in range(n):
                if matrix[r][c].isupper():
                    portals[matrix[r][c]].append((r, c))
        INF = float("inf")
        dist = [[INF] * n for _ in range(m)]
        dist[0][0] = 0
        dq = deque([(0, 0)])
        used = set()
        while dq:
            r, c = dq.popleft()
            d = dist[r][c]
            if (r, c) == (m - 1, n - 1):
                return d
            ch = matrix[r][c]
            if ch.isupper() and ch not in used:
                used.add(ch)  # this letter's teleport is spent here, at its cheapest
                for pr, pc in portals[ch]:
                    if d < dist[pr][pc]:
                        dist[pr][pc] = d
                        dq.appendleft((pr, pc))  # free move: same distance
            for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                if 0 <= nr < m and 0 <= nc < n and matrix[nr][nc] != "#" and d + 1 < dist[nr][nc]:
                    dist[nr][nc] = d + 1
                    dq.append((nr, nc))
        return -1
function minMoves(matrix: string[]): number {
    const m = matrix.length, n = matrix[0].length;
    const isUpper = (ch: string): boolean => ch >= "A" && ch <= "Z";
    const portals = new Map<string, [number, number][]>();
    for (let r = 0; r < m; r++) {
        for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            if (isUpper(matrix[r][c])) {
                if (!portals.has(matrix[r][c])) {
                    portals.set(matrix[r][c], []);
                }
                portals.get(matrix[r][c])!.push([r, c]);
            }
        }
    }
    const dist: number[][] = Array.from({ length: m }, () => new Array(n).fill(Infinity));
    dist[0][0] = 0;
    const dq: [number, number][] = [[0, 0]];  // 0-1 BFS: free moves go to the front
    const used = new Set<string>();
    while (dq.length > 0) {
        const [r, c] = dq.shift()!;
        const d = dist[r][c];
        if (r === m - 1 && c === n - 1) {
            return d;
        }
        const ch = matrix[r][c];
        if (isUpper(ch) && !used.has(ch)) {
            used.add(ch);  // this letter's teleport is spent here, at its cheapest
            for (const [pr, pc] of portals.get(ch)!) {
                if (d < dist[pr][pc]) {
                    dist[pr][pc] = d;
                    dq.unshift([pr, pc]);  // free move: same distance
                }
            }
        }
        for (const [nr, nc] of [[r + 1, c], [r - 1, c], [r, c + 1], [r, c - 1]]) {
            if (0 <= nr && nr < m && 0 <= nc && nc < n && matrix[nr][nc] !== "#" && d + 1 < dist[nr][nc]) {
                dist[nr][nc] = d + 1;
                dq.push([nr, nc]);
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int minMoves(String[] matrix) {
        int m = matrix.length, n = matrix[0].length();
        Map<Character, List<int[]>> portals = new HashMap<>();
        for (int r = 0; r < m; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                char ch = matrix[r].charAt(c);
                if (Character.isUpperCase(ch)) {
                    portals.computeIfAbsent(ch, key -> new ArrayList<>()).add(new int[] {r, c});
                }
            }
        }
        final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        int[][] dist = new int[m][n];
        for (int[] row : dist) {
            Arrays.fill(row, INF);
        }
        dist[0][0] = 0;
        Deque<int[]> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();  // 0-1 BFS: free moves go to the front
        dq.offer(new int[] {0, 0});
        Set<Character> used = new HashSet<>();
        int[][] dirs = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
        while (!dq.isEmpty()) {
            int[] cell = dq.pollFirst();
            int r = cell[0], c = cell[1];
            int d = dist[r][c];
            if (r == m - 1 && c == n - 1) {
                return d;
            }
            char ch = matrix[r].charAt(c);
            if (Character.isUpperCase(ch) && !used.contains(ch)) {
                used.add(ch);  // this letter's teleport is spent here, at its cheapest
                for (int[] p : portals.get(ch)) {
                    if (d < dist[p[0]][p[1]]) {
                        dist[p[0]][p[1]] = d;
                        dq.offerFirst(new int[] {p[0], p[1]});  // free move: same distance
                    }
                }
            }
            for (int[] dd : dirs) {
                int nr = r + dd[0], nc = c + dd[1];
                if (0 <= nr && nr < m && 0 <= nc && nc < n && matrix[nr].charAt(nc) != '#' && d + 1 < dist[nr][nc]) {
                    dist[nr][nc] = d + 1;
                    dq.offerLast(new int[] {nr, nc});
                }
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The deque stays sorted by distance: zero-cost teleports go to the front, moves to the back.
  2. The first time a letter is popped is at its smallest distance, so teleporting from there dominates any later use; the once-per-letter rule never hurts.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Start or end on a portal.
  • Unreachable end → −1.
  • Portals behind walls.

Complexity: O(m · n) time and space.

Hard 854. K-Similar Strings Amazon StringQueueHash Set

Problem: Return the fewest swaps of two letters to turn s1 into the anagram s2.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s1 = "ab", s2 = "ba"
Output: 1
Explanation: The two string are 1-similar because we can use one swap to change s1 to s2: "ab" --> "ba".
Example 2
Input: s1 = "abc", s2 = "bca"
Output: 2
Explanation: The two strings are 2-similar because we can use two swaps to change s1 to s2: "abc" --> "bac" --> "bca".

Constraints: 1 ≤ s1.length ≤ 20 · s2.length == s1.length · s1 and s2 contain only lowercase letters from the set {'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f'}. · s2 is an anagram of s1.

Hint 1

Model each string as a BFS state and each swap as an edge.

Hint 2

Reduce branching: always fix the first wrong position.

From brute force to the pattern: BFS with all O(n²) swaps explodes; fixing the first mismatch keeps the search small.

Spot it: Fewest swaps → BFS where each state is a string. Branching is cut down by always fixing the first mismatch i: swap it with a later j where cur[j] == s2[i] (and preferably cur[j] != s2[j]).

Why not another pattern? Greedy swapping isn't optimal when cycles of length > 2 exist; trying all swaps is far too many states.

Approach:

  1. Queue starts with s1, distance 0.
  2. Pop cur; find the first i with cur[i] != s2[i].
  3. For each j > i with cur[j] == s2[i] and cur[j] != s2[j]: swap, enqueue if new.
  4. Return the distance when cur == s2.
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def kSimilarity(self, s1: str, s2: str) -> int:
        seen = {s1}
        queue = deque([(s1, 0)])
        while queue:
            cur, swaps = queue.popleft()
            if cur == s2:
                return swaps
            i = 0
            while cur[i] == s2[i]:
                i += 1  # first position that's wrong
            for j in range(i + 1, len(cur)):
                if cur[j] == s2[i] and cur[j] != s2[j]:  # brings the right letter to i, and j was wrong anyway
                    nxt = cur[:i] + cur[j] + cur[i + 1:j] + cur[i] + cur[j + 1:]
                    if nxt not in seen:
                        seen.add(nxt)
                        queue.append((nxt, swaps + 1))
        return -1
function kSimilarity(s1: string, s2: string): number {
    const seen = new Set<string>([s1]);
    const queue: [string, number][] = [[s1, 0]];
    let head = 0;  // queue[head] is the front; shift() would be O(n)
    while (head < queue.length) {
        const [cur, swaps] = queue[head++];
        if (cur === s2) {
            return swaps;
        }
        let i = 0;
        while (cur[i] === s2[i]) {
            i += 1;  // first position that's wrong
        }
        for (let j = i + 1; j < cur.length; j++) {
            if (cur[j] === s2[i] && cur[j] !== s2[j]) {  // brings the right letter to i, and j was wrong anyway
                const nxt = cur.slice(0, i) + cur[j] + cur.slice(i + 1, j) + cur[i] + cur.slice(j + 1);
                if (!seen.has(nxt)) {
                    seen.add(nxt);
                    queue.push([nxt, swaps + 1]);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int kSimilarity(String s1, String s2) {
        Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>(Set.of(s1));
        Deque<Object[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.offer(new Object[] {s1, 0});
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            Object[] item = queue.poll();
            String cur = (String) item[0];
            int swaps = (Integer) item[1];
            if (cur.equals(s2)) {
                return swaps;
            }
            int i = 0;
            while (cur.charAt(i) == s2.charAt(i)) {
                i += 1;  // first position that's wrong
            }
            for (int j = i + 1; j < cur.length(); j++) {
                if (cur.charAt(j) == s2.charAt(i) && cur.charAt(j) != s2.charAt(j)) {  // brings the right letter to i, and j was wrong anyway
                    String nxt = cur.substring(0, i) + cur.charAt(j) + cur.substring(i + 1, j) + cur.charAt(i) + cur.substring(j + 1);
                    if (!seen.contains(nxt)) {
                        seen.add(nxt);
                        queue.offer(new Object[] {nxt, swaps + 1});
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Fixing the first mismatch first doesn't lose optimality: some optimal sequence fixes it with one of these swaps.
  2. Skipping j that are already correct avoids pointless moves.
  3. BFS returns the fewest swaps.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Already equal → 0.
  • A 2-cycle (one swap).
  • Long cycles of letters.

Complexity: Exponential in the worst case but small for length ≤ 20 with this pruning.

Medium 1197. Minimum Knight Moves Apple QueueHash Set

Problem: On an infinite board, return the fewest knight moves from (0, 0) to (x, y).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ (Premium)

Example 1
Input: x = 2, y = 1
Output: 1
Explanation: One move: [0, 0] → [2, 1].
Example 2
Input: x = 5, y = 5
Output: 4
Explanation: [0, 0] → [2, 1] → [4, 2] → [3, 4] → [5, 5].

Constraints: -300 ≤ x, y ≤ 300 · 0 ≤ |x| + |y| ≤ 300

Hint 1

Shortest number of moves: BFS.

Hint 2

Use symmetry to search only one quadrant (with a small margin).

From brute force to the pattern: Unbounded BFS in all quadrants works but explores 4× more; symmetry trims it.

Spot it: Fewest moves on an unweighted graph → BFS. By symmetry, target (|x|, |y|) and stay in the first quadrant, allowing coordinates down to −2 (some shortest paths dip slightly below the axes).

Why not another pattern? DFS doesn't find shortest paths; an unbounded BFS explores four quadrants for nothing.

Approach:

  1. x, y = |x|, |y|.
  2. BFS from (0, 0) with the 8 knight moves, skipping cells with a coordinate below −2.
  3. Return the distance when the target is reached.
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def minKnightMoves(self, x: int, y: int) -> int:
        x, y = abs(x), abs(y)  # all four quadrants look the same
        moves = [(1, 2), (2, 1), (2, -1), (1, -2), (-1, -2), (-2, -1), (-2, 1), (-1, 2)]
        seen = {(0, 0)}
        queue = deque([(0, 0, 0)])
        while queue:
            r, c, d = queue.popleft()
            if (r, c) == (x, y):
                return d
            for dr, dc in moves:
                nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
                if nr >= -2 and nc >= -2 and (nr, nc) not in seen:  # small dip below the axes is enough
                    seen.add((nr, nc))
                    queue.append((nr, nc, d + 1))
        return -1
function minKnightMoves(x: number, y: number): number {
    x = Math.abs(x);  // all four quadrants look the same
    y = Math.abs(y);
    const moves = [[1, 2], [2, 1], [2, -1], [1, -2], [-1, -2], [-2, -1], [-2, 1], [-1, 2]];
    const seen = new Set<string>(["0,0"]);
    const queue: [number, number, number][] = [[0, 0, 0]];
    let head = 0;  // queue[head] is the front; shift() would be O(n)
    while (head < queue.length) {
        const [r, c, d] = queue[head++];
        if (r === x && c === y) {
            return d;
        }
        for (const [dr, dc] of moves) {
            const nr = r + dr, nc = c + dc;
            if (nr >= -2 && nc >= -2 && !seen.has(`${nr},${nc}`)) {  // small dip below the axes is enough
                seen.add(`${nr},${nc}`);
                queue.push([nr, nc, d + 1]);
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int minKnightMoves(int x, int y) {
        x = Math.abs(x);  // all four quadrants look the same
        y = Math.abs(y);
        int[][] moves = {{1, 2}, {2, 1}, {2, -1}, {1, -2}, {-1, -2}, {-2, -1}, {-2, 1}, {-1, 2}};
        Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>(Set.of("0,0"));
        Deque<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.offer(new int[] {0, 0, 0});
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            int[] item = queue.poll();
            int r = item[0], c = item[1], d = item[2];
            if (r == x && c == y) {
                return d;
            }
            for (int[] m : moves) {
                int nr = r + m[0], nc = c + m[1];
                String key = nr + "," + nc;
                if (nr >= -2 && nc >= -2 && !seen.contains(key)) {  // small dip below the axes is enough
                    seen.add(key);
                    queue.offer(new int[] {nr, nc, d + 1});
                }
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Reflecting the target into the first quadrant doesn't change the answer.
  2. Paths to targets near the origin (like (1, 1)) need to step to negative coordinates, but never below −2.
  3. BFS returns the shortest distance.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Target (0, 0) → 0.
  • (1, 1) → 2.
  • Far targets.

Complexity: O(|x| · |y|) time and space.
